item.title: Cockroaches found in food, cats sleeping in food prep areas
item.description:
Nurul Absar, a resident of Khaja Road in Chattogram, had been suffering from diarrhoea for two days. His health did not improve a bit even after drinking coconut water and saline. As he grew physically weaker, he went to the local Gausul Azam Urban Dispensary for medical advice.

Nurul Absar was speaking in front of the dispensary on Tuesday morning. His wife Rehana Begum was also with him. She said, as her husband is often away from home for work, he has to eat lunch at hotels and restaurants almost every day. His condition had deteriorated two days earlier.

The exact cause of Nurul Absar’s illness could not be confirmed. However, many people in Chattogram like him rely on hotels and restaurants for their daily meals. Working people, students, job seekers and even people visiting the city for various purposes dine at these eateries.

Recent drives by government agencies across hotels and restaurants in the city have uncovered various irregularities in food preparation and storage. Live and dead cockroaches were found in food ingredients in some places. Insects were found roaming around in kitchens as well.

Some restaurants were preparing food beside open dustbins, storing raw and cooked meat together and preparing meals in unhygienic conditions. There have also been allegations of using burnt oil and expired ingredients. There are also allegations of using burnt oil and expired ingredients. In one hotel, a cat was even found lying inside the place used for food preparation.

Doctors say contaminated food can cause various foodborne illnesses, including diarrhoea, vomiting and abdominal pain. Preparing food in unhygienic conditions and failing to store it properly after cooking increases the risk of bacterial contamination.

Cockroaches in food, irregularities in kitchens

During drives at various hotels and restaurants in Chattogram city in September, the Bangladesh Food Safety Authority (BFSA) found live and dead cockroaches and bedbugs in food ingredients. The insects were found in dalda (hydrogenated vegetable oil), raisins, milk, murabba (preserve), oil, spices and dough used to make bread. Kitchens and food storage areas were also found to be unhygienic.

The drives also detected irregularities such as placing open dustbins inside kitchens and storing raw and cooked meat together. In August, food safety officials discovered a cat lying in the food preparation area inside the kitchen of Al-Helal Hotel and Restaurant at the busy GEC intersection in the city.

According to officials of the food safety authority, at least 42 establishments have been fined more than Tk 15 million in total this year. The penalties were imposed over allegations including food adulteration, unhygienic conditions and the use of unauthorised ingredients in food preparation. The list of such eateries includes Sadia’s Kitchen, Barcode, Home Recipe Foods, Kacchi Dine and a KFC outlet.

Mohammad Farhan Islam, the Metropolitan Safe Food Officer of the Bangladesh Safe Food Authority (BSFA) told Prothom Alo that food preparation areas, the storage of ingredients, kitchen hygiene and food handlers’ personal hygiene are directly linked to public health. The insect's presence in food preparation areas in particular increases the risk of food contamination.

Unsafe food even beside hospitals

On 1 October, a drive by the Directorate of National Consumer Rights Protection in the Chattogram Medical College Hospital area uncovered various irregularities at CMC Cafe and the canteen for fourth-class employees. Raw fish and meat were being stored alongside cooked food in the cafe’s refrigerator. Cockroaches were found in the dough used to make bread at the employees’ canteen.

Mohammad Faiz Ullah, deputy director of the Chattogram District Office of DNCRP said, irregularities in food preparation and storage in places such as hospitals can pose health risks to patients and their relatives. Storing cooked food with raw fish and meat and preparing food in unhygienic conditions increase the risk of contamination by germs.

Mohammad Abdur Rob, associate professor of medicine at Chattogram Medical College Hospital, told Prothom Alo that consuming contaminated food, drinking contaminated water increases the risk of diarrhoea. People should pay attention not only to the types of food they eat but also to where and under what conditions it is prepared. Unclean food preparation areas can pose health risks, he said.

Doctors say diarrhoea causes the body to lose water and salts. It is therefore important to drink adequate amounts of oral rehydration saline and safe water from the outset. Medical advice should be sought if the condition worsens.

item.title: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia fired in less than a week after facing criticism
item.description:
USA-TRUMP/ZACHARIA

White House press secretary Katie Zacharia was fired after less than a week on the job, two US officials said on Friday, after a rocky start as President Donald Trump's top spokesperson.

Zacharia was "let go" and is "transitioning out" of the press secretary position, according to two separate White House officials. She faced days of questions about her legal credentials and criticism of her performance in a news briefing and interviews.

The departure leaves Trump without a key public messenger just over two weeks before November's midterm elections, a critical period when the president is seeking to tout his administration's accomplishments and help his fellow Republicans retain control of Congress.

Trump told reporters earlier on Friday that he had asked Zacharia to reconsider whether to continue in her role after facing tough press coverage during her first days on the job.

"I told her: 'I think you're better off being happy, and I'm not sure you can ever be happy in this stuff.' There's nothing easy about this stuff," Trump told reporters as he departed the White House for a weekend trip.

He added: "I said to her honestly, 'If I were you, I'd reconsider... think about it. But I would reconsider.'" Trump said he intended to revisit the conversation with Zacharia later.

Zacharia started on Monday and held her debut White House briefing on Tuesday. She said she received a call about the press secretary role on October 7 and was offered the job to succeed Karoline Leavitt a week ago.

She soon faced questions about her career, which she said included a tenure practicing law. Trump had also described her as an attorney.

"I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials," Zacharia said in an emailed statement on Wednesday.

Reuters could not find records showing the Pepperdine University law school graduate was registered as an attorney or member of the bar in any US state or the District of Columbia.

During a Fox News interview on Thursday, Zacharia said she did not pass the barexam. Law school graduates cannot legally practice law in the US without first being admitted to a state bar.

Zacharia and the White House did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment about her firing.

Earlier on Friday, she told reporters at the White House that she was looking forward to working with the press.

Trump hired Zacharia after expressing concerns about the media coverage of his administration, feeling he needed a new spokesperson who could amplify his achievements, according to two people familiar with the conversations.

In a phone interview with Fox on Friday, Trump said he was in no rush to name a new press secretary.

Zacharia's quick exit meant she had what is believed to be the shortest tenure of any press secretary in the role's history.

"Records are made to be broken," Anthony Scaramucci, who served as director of communications for 10 days during Trump's first administration, said on X. "But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."

item.title: California city council elections: 3 Bangladeshi-Americans run in 3 cities
item.description:
Bangladeshi-Americans are stepping forward to boost their representation in mainstream US politics. In line with this, three Bangladeshi-Americans are running in City Council elections across three cities in California.

They are Shazia Hoq in Montebello (Los Angeles County), Mohammed Rahman in Perris (Riverside County) and M S Alam in Chino (San Bernardino County).

Members of the local Bangladeshi-American community have rallied behind the three candidates. Some are providing financial assistance, others are helping raise campaign funds, while many are offering personal encouragement and moral support.

Their involvement is helping the candidates run their campaigns and giving the Bangladeshi community an opportunity to strengthen its presence in local US politics.

The three candidates of Bangladeshi origin are actively campaigning to win seats on their respective city councils in the elections scheduled for 3 November.

Shazia calls for joining mainstream politics

Shazia Hoq is running for the City Council from District 1 in Montebello, Los Angeles County. Her rivals in the race are Georgina Tamayo, Kimberly Cobos Cawthorne and Rafael Santoya.

Being involved in business, writing and community leadership, Shazia Hoq has long taken part in social and civic initiatives. According to her, she brings nearly 20 years of experience working across business and community sectors.

In her campaign, Shazia Hoq emphasizes transparency and accountability in city administration, responsible budget management, safer neighborhoods and support for local businesses. Her goal is to ensure residents have a real voice in city decisions and receive reliable municipal services.

When asked why she entered local US politics, Shazia Hoq told Prothom Alo, "As a Bangladeshi-American woman, I feel we are far behind other ethnic groups in America. Since we live here, we must get involved in mainstream politics to benefit from what America offers and we need to lead the way for the next generation."

Mohammed Rahman confident of victory

Mohammed Rahman is contesting for the City Council from District 1 in Perris, Riverside County. His opponents are Guadalupe Gomez and Juan Carlos (JC) Franco.

Mohammed Rahman has worked with the United States Postal Service (USPS) for 27 years. Over his long career, he had the opportunity to interact with people from diverse communities, an experience he says is proving very helpful on the campaign trail.

Speaking about his campaign, Mohammed Rahman told Prothom Alo that the name recognition built through his postal career is helping him connect with voters and he remains optimistic about winning.

Mohammed Rahman's platform focuses on public safety, affordable housing, small business growth and creating more opportunities for young people. He is also emphasizing neighborhood amenities, including community policing, neighborhood watch programs, adequate street lighting and better sidewalks.

M S Alam seeks to leverage experience

M S Alam is running for the City Council from District 3 in Chino, San Bernardino County. His opponent is incumbent Council Member Marc Lucio.

An engineer by profession, M S Alam works as a full-time project manager in District 7 of the California Department of Transportation (Caltrans). He also teaches part-time at California State University, Long Beach and has conducted transportation engineering research and doctoral-level work at UCLA. He has been living in Chino for 18 years.

The main themes of Alam's campaign include safe and planned urbanization, better transit systems, strong infrastructure, responsible development and quality civic services. He believes city development should meet current residents' needs while creating opportunities for future generations.

When asked about delivering on his platform, M S Alam told Prothom Alo that he would work hard to implement the promises outlined in his campaign manifesto.

Significance of the Bangladeshi community support

While the election contexts differ for the three candidates, they share a common goal. Increasing Bangladeshi-American participation in local politics.

Shazia Hoq focuses on the participation of Bangladeshi-American women in mainstream politics. Mohammed Rahman prioritizes housing, public safety and neighborhood welfare. Meanwhile, M S Alam brings forward his engineering and project management background to advocate for planned urbanization and infrastructure growth.

In the United States, City Council decisions directly affect residents' everyday lives such as shaping roads, transit, housing, public safety, urban planning, local commerce and basic municipal services. As a result, the choices made by council members closely touch local livelihoods.

On 3 November, voters in Montebello, Perris and Chino will decide who represents them on their city councils. For these three Bangladeshi-American candidates, the race is not just about winning an election, but about securing a seat at the decision-making table for the Bangladeshi community.

item.title: Durga Puja: Maha Saptami today
item.description:
The Hindu community of Bangladesh is celebrating Maha Saptami today on 17 October, the second day of the six-day Sharodiyo Durgotsab, as the tithi (lunar day) of Maha Saptami spans two days this year.

The extended observance of Maha Saptami will continue tomorrow.

The day began with the Nabapatrika ritual, in which nine plants representing different forms of Goddess Durga are ceremonially bathed and worshipped. Devotees are also offering anjali after the Saptami puja at temples across the country.

Earlier, Maha Shashthi, the first day of Durga Puja, was celebrated on Friday with Bodhan, the ceremonial awakening and invocation of Goddess Durga, marking the formal commencement of the festivities.

Since morning, devotees have been thronging temples and makeshift puja mandaps across the country, with Dhakeshwari National Temple emerging as a focal point of the celebrations in the capital.

Various religious rituals, including Kalparambha and Bihit Puja, were held at the temple in the morning as the six-day festival will continue until 21 October.

Mahanagar Sarbajanin Puja Committee General Secretary Suvasish Kumar Biswas Sadhan said the festival began with Maha Shashthi puja, followed by anjali offerings by devotees and distribution of prasad.

Clothes were also distributed among underprivileged people on the occasion.

According to traditional beliefs, Goddess Durga arrives this year on a horse (ghotak), symbolising dry spells, heavy rainfall or an unstable period, and departs on a boat (noka), signifying a bumper harvest and agricultural prosperity.

A total of 33,851 puja mandaps have been set up across the country this year, including 258 in Dhaka, according to the Bangladesh Puja Udjapan Parishad. The number of mandaps has increased by nearly 1,500 compared with last year.

The Gulshan-Banani Puja Foundation is hosting one of the most elaborate celebrations at Kemal Ataturk Park in Banani, where this year's theme, 'Jalaja', draws inspiration from water as a source of life, creation and divine power.

The mandap features an aquatic-inspired design incorporating traditional crafts, lighting and decorative elements to create an immersive experience for visitors. Pandal hoppers are moving from one venue to another to admire religious art, illuminated displays and creative cultural themes.

Makeshift pandals at Kalabagan ground and Khamarbari have also emerged as major attractions for visitors in the capital. Large temporary mandaps and eye-catching lighting displays are drawing crowds to the venues.

Maha Ashtami will be observed on Monday, with Kumari Puja scheduled at several mandaps. During the ritual, an unmarried pre-pubescent girl, generally aged between one and 16, is worshipped as the living embodiment of the divine feminine and Goddess Durga.

Sandhi Puja will also be held on Monday evening at the transitional moment between Ashtami and Navami. According to Hindu mythology, the ritual commemorates the moment Goddess Durga assumed the form of Chamunda to slay the demon brothers Chanda and Munda.

Devotees will observe Maha Navami on Tuesday with religious fervour and enthusiasm. They will gather at puja mandaps and pandals to offer flowers, water, clothes and ornaments to the deity. The day will feature major concluding worship rituals and the offering of bhog.

On Wednesday, Maha Dashami will be observed, marking the farewell to Goddess Durga. Devotees will take the idols in processions to designated rivers, ponds and other water bodies for immersion, known as Bisarjan.

This year, the government has extended the Durga Puja holiday to three days through an executive order in response to longstanding demands from the Hindu community.

Combined with the regular Friday and Saturday weekend holidays, the extended holiday will provide a five-day break from 20 October to 24 October.

Bangladesh Puja Udjapan Parishad President Basudeb Dhar thanked Prime Minister Tarique Rahman for extending the holiday on the occasion.

Durga Puja holds deep religious and cultural significance for Bangladesh's Hindu community. The festival commemorates Goddess Durga's victory over the demon king Mahishasura and symbolises the triumph of good over evil.

According to Hindu mythology, the deities combined their divine powers to create Goddess Durga, who fought and ultimately defeated Mahishasura.

Beyond its religious significance, Durga Puja is an integral part of Bangladesh's cultural heritage. The festival brings together members of the Hindu community and people of other faiths, reflecting the country's tradition of communal harmony and peaceful coexistence.

The government has increased the allocation for Durga Puja mandaps to Tk 50 million from Tk 40 million. The rice allocation has also been raised to 600 kilogrammes per mandap from 500 kilogrammes in previous years.

Necessary security measures have been taken nationwide to ensure peaceful and smooth celebrations.

The authorities will use a mobile application previously deployed by the National Telecommunication Monitoring Centre (NTMC) to strengthen monitoring during the festival. The application will facilitate the rapid dissemination of information about any untoward incident and help authorities respond promptly to maintain a peaceful and festive environment.

The Home Ministry has also instructed the relevant authorities to ensure uninterrupted electricity supply to puja venues. Mandap organisers have been asked to keep generators on standby round the clock and maintain rechargeable lights as backup in case of power outages or generator failures.

item.title: Bangladesh ranks 7th globally in footwear manufacturing, China on top
item.description:
The world’s population currently stands at around 8.28 billion. Last year, an average of three pairs of shoes were made for every person, bringing global footwear production to 24.6 billion pairs. Asian countries manufactured 88.7 per cent of the total.

China retained its position as the world’s largest footwear manufacturer, manufacturing 13.66 billion pairs last year. India and Vietnam ranked second and third respectively, while Bangladesh emerged as the world’s seventh-largest footwear manufacturer, making around 554 million pairs in 2025.

These figures are from the World Footwear Yearbook 2026, published under the initiative of the Portuguese Footwear, Components and Leather Goods Manufacturers’ Association (APICCAPS).

According to the report, global footwear production fell by 0.1 per cent to 24.6 billion pairs in 2025. In 2024 however, the production had increased by nearly 10 per cent.

Who produces the most footwear

Ten countries account for 89.5 per cent of the world’s annual footwear production. China alone accounts for 55.6 per cent of the total, having produced 13.66 billion pairs last year. India, in second place, manufactured 3 billion pairs, representing 12.2 per cent of global production.

Vietnam is the world’s third-largest footwear manufacturer. It manufactured 1.658 billion pairs last year. Brazil, Indonesia and Pakistan ranked fourth, fifth and sixth, producing 848 million, 782 million and 627 million pairs respectively.

Meanwhile, Bangladesh ranked seventh, producing 554 million pairs in 2025 and accounting for 2.3 per cent of global footwear production. Turkey, Cambodia and Mexico completed the list of the world’s top 10 footwear-producing countries.

China’s share of footwear exports declines

Asian countries dominate global footwear exports, accounting for 84.3 per cent of all pairs exported worldwide. However, Bangladesh did not make the list of the world’s top 10 footwear exporters. The leading exporters are China, Vietnam, Indonesia, Germany, India, Cambodia, Belgium, Netherlands, Italy and Turkey.

China exported around 9.01 billion pairs of shoes last year, accounting for 61.2 per cent of global footwear exports. A decade earlier in 2016, China’s share stood at 69.1 per cent. Rising labour costs, trade wars and other factors have contributed to the decline, with Vietnam capturing a significant portion of the business China has lost.

Vietnam exported 1.66 billion pairs of shoes last year, accounting for 11.2 per cent of global footwear exports. Indonesia exported 580 million pairs, Germany 360 million and India 270 million.

According to the World Footwear Yearbook, Europe accounted for 13.1 per cent of global footwear exports. However, European exporters earned more per pair than their Asian counterparts. The average export price was $34.76 per pair in Europe, compared with $8.02 in Asia.

Europe was also the world’s largest destination for footwear imports. The continent accounted for 35.3 per cent of total global footwear imports last year.

Asia’s share was 25.5 per cent, while North America accounted for 20.3 per cent.

North America’s share of global footwear imports has declined from 23.3 per cent in 2016. In contrast, the shares of Africa and South America have increased.

Asia has the highest footwear demand

Asia was the world’s largest footwear consumption market in 2025, accounting for 56 per cent of all shoes used worldwide. The region’s growing share of the global market highlights the footwear industry’s increasing shift towards Asia, driven by both manufacturers and consumers.

However, Asia’s high overall footwear consumption is driven more by its large population than by per capita use. In 2025, people in Asia used an average of 2.6 pairs of shoes per person, considerably less than in developed and mature markets.

North America recorded the highest per capita footwear consumption last year, with each person using an average of 4.6 pairs. The average in Europe was 4.1 pairs.

In Africa, by contrast, per capita footwear consumption stood at just 1.6 pairs. This indicates that limited purchasing power and the affordability of footwear remain major barriers to growth in demand across the continent.

item.title: India protests: Cockroach movement founder Abhijeet Dipke arrested, activist Neha Bora released
item.description:
INDIA-POLITICS/

Police arrested Indian "cockroach" movement founder Abhijeet Dipke, according to several media reports on Saturday, after he was detained on Friday ahead of a Delhi rally that drew hundreds of people waving the national flag and demanding the resignation of India's election chief.

Dipke was arrested to prevent a breach of the peace and will be called before a Special Executive Magistrate on Saturday, broadcasters NDTV and India Today said.

Delhi police did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment.

The youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), opposition groups and student organisations have held near-daily protests this month demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation over a revision of voter lists that they say favours Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

More than 130 million voters were deleted during the revision. The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol. The BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.

Student activist Neha Bora, a prominent face of the protests, who was also detained on Friday as she tried to reach central Delhi with dozens of supporters, was released on Saturday.

"Please, spare the people of India. Impeach Gyanesh Kumar and halt SIR (special intensive revision), so that the ordinary citizens of this country can breathe a sigh of relief, feel at ease, and have their voting rights ensured," Bora told ANI news agency after she was released.

Dipke was detained on Friday as he stepped out of a house in central Delhi, with police hauling him into a police car and driving away after a brief argument.

Dipke had called Friday's protest in support of two CJP leaders detained and sent to jail this week for five days for demonstrating at a protest site in violation of a ban.

Earlier on Friday, police had met Dipke and warned him against going ahead with the protest.

The cockroach movement has emerged as one of the biggest political challenges faced by Modi and the BJP in the prime minister's 12 years in power.

A weeks-long sit-in by supporters of the movement earlier this year forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation over exam paper leaks.

item.title: Raazi: A gripping tale of unsung heroes
item.description:
Investigators find espionage equipment hidden in Abdul’s room after meticulously searching it following his mysterious death. Iqbal notices a tiny, sparkling object lying on the floor which he soon realizes is a broken ghungroo from the anklet he had gifted his beloved wife. His heart skips a beat. A wave of dread washes over him. Will Sehmat be able to conceal her true identity from her in-laws anymore?

This climactic scene was from Raazi (2018), directed by Meghna Gulzar, an adaptation of Harinder Sikka’s novel “Calling Sehmat” — a true-life story involving a 20-year-old Indian college student who becomes an undercover agent in Pakistan before the 1971 war.

The Plot 

Hidayat Khan is an Indian freedom fighter and businessman in Kashmir who works with Indian Intelligence (RAW). Upon being cognizant of his deteriorating health, his 20-year-old daughter, Sehmat (Alia Bhatt) agrees to fulfill his dying wish. He wants her to get married into a prominent Pakistani military family in order to serve as an informant. Sehmat undergoes a period of intense spy training in Morse code, combat, and espionage with the help of Khalid Mir, a senior RAW officer.

Soon afterwards, Sehmat marries Iqbal Syed (Vicky Kaushal), the youngest son of a high-ranking Pakistani military general, Brigadier Parvez Syed. While maintaining the status of the daughter-in-law of the Syed family, Sehmat surreptitiously gathers classified naval and military plans. She uses a radio transmitter to send vital secrets back to her handlers in India as the tension between the two nations escalates.

Things were on the verge of getting more complicated as a loyal servant member Abdul discovers her true identity. His suspicion of her was evident from the very beginning. She is forced to commit extreme acts of espionage and elimination to protect her cover, as instructed by Khalid Mir.

Eventually, her husband Iqbal is appalled when he discovers that she is an Indian spy. Her handlers try to extract her which leads to a perilous climax.

Resolution

Sehmat survives and escapes back to India. The critical intelligence she provided helped the Indian Navy sink a Pakistani submarine and win key naval advantages. This played a pivotal role in shifting the dynamic of the war in favor of India.

Sehmat is deeply scarred by her experience when she returns to India, pregnant with Iqbal’s child.

Reflection

An important theme that resonates throughout the movie is that nothing is more important than one’s motherland. The film commemorates the 1971 war, where many people like Sehmat demonstrated unwavering and laudable courage.

I really enjoyed watching it because it was highly suspenseful and entertaining. I feel like it would be a crime not to mention how praiseworthy Alia’s performance was. She did a tremendous job bringing Sehmat’s character to life. Beyond her acts of bravery, Alia captured the character’s vulnerable side exceptionally well.

There are moments where she feels completely isolated. She breaks down in tears when she can no longer hold it in, feeling deeply torn between her duty and her personal life. I’m definitely inspired to watch more of her movies after this. Moreover, viewers adored the tender chemistry between Alia and Vicky.

Not to mention, the beautiful track ‘Dilbaro’ absolutely stole my heart.

Interestingly, there is an entire genre in Bollywood that can informally be labeled as ‘nationalistic’ or ‘patriotic’ or to be more direct— ‘anti-Pakistan.’ There are Indian movies that carry a message of peace and reconciliation like, perhaps, Bajrangi Bhaijaan. Raazi, of course, has a different twist. Critics ask whether such films should serve to foster regional peace and mutual understanding or deepen the divide. Or is it just telling a story.

Whatever the deeper implications may be, it's a well-made film which I highly recommend watching.

* Fabliha Fariha is a student of International Hope School

item.title: DSCC: Drivers draw salaries, others drive garbage trucks, costing lives
item.description:
It was around 12:45 am on 4 October. A garbage truck belonging to Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) arrived at the municipal filling station in Sayedabad to refuel. This correspondent went closer and found that the young man sitting in the driver's seat was not the driver listed in the records. The vehicle had been assigned to Sardar Humayun Kabir but was being driven by Saju Ahmed. He is an outsider, not an employee of the corporation. He works as an assistant for Tk 10,000 a month. Although he had driven the heavy vehicle to the filling station, he claimed to have a licence for light vehicles.

When asked where the assigned driver was, Saju initially said he was nearby. Asked again, he said his uncle was chatting at Golapbagh intersection. A little later, he drove away without refuelling. He also alerted other drivers about the presence of a journalist. I then waited at the filling station for nearly two hours, but no other DSCC vehicle arrived to refuel.

Nearly five years ago, Notre Dame College student Naim Hasan was killed after being run over by a DSCC garbage truck. That vehicle, too, was being driven by someone other than its assigned driver. Despite student protests, the occupation of Nagar Bhaban, investigations and the suspension of the driver, the practice of handing over vehicle keys to others has not stopped. Similar irregularities were also found in the deaths of school student Mahin Ahmed and laundry shop employee Iqbal Hossain.

In an investigation into the waste transport vehicles of DSCC, Prothom Alo found that 22 vehicles were being driven by people other than their assigned drivers. According to relevant sources, the actual number of such vehicles is at least 56. Some of the drivers to whom the vehicles have been assigned are drawing salaries without driving them themselves. Their assistants or outsiders are driving the vehicles instead. There are also allegations that the drivers do not collect the full amount of fuel allocated to them and share the money equivalent to the remaining fuel.

The investigation found that at least 16 people had died in 15 fatal accidents involving DSCC garbage trucks between 2018 and 4 October this year. Two more people were killed in an accident in Basabo the previous year. In total, at least 18 people have died in 16 accidents since 2017. In at least three of these incidents, the vehicles were being driven by people other than their assigned drivers.

Shah Alam Talukder, president of the DSCC Transport Drivers, Workers and Employees Union, did not completely deny the irregularities.

He told Prothom Alo that others are sometimes allowed to drive the vehicles. In his words, “I cannot say that everything is absolutely fine. There are certainly mistakes.”

However, he said that after journalists began investigating, they had also started monitoring the situation themselves and assistants were no longer being allowed to drive the vehicles.

DSCC Administrator Md Abdus Salam told Prothom Alo that one accident had occurred since he took charge. However, questioning why even one person should die in such an accident, he said he had instructed officials not to allow anyone without a driving licence to operate the vehicles.

If an assistant is allowed to drive a vehicle, action will be taken against both the assigned driver and the official responsible for supervising them, he added.

Assigned driver chatting, assistant behind the wheel

To verify reports that outsiders were driving garbage trucks, this correspondent went to the municipal filling station in Sayedabad around 11:00 pm on 4 October. The corporation's vehicles refuel at this pump, which it owns, although outside vehicles can also buy fuel there. This correspondent waited at the station to match vehicle registration numbers with the identities of their assigned drivers. At around 12:45 am, 5 October a vehicle bearing registration number 11-4303 arrived.

According to the corporation's records, the vehicle was assigned to heavy vehicle driver Sardar Humayun Kabir. Saju Ahmed, who was sitting in the driver's seat, said he was not an employee of the corporation. He receives Tk 10,000 a month as an assistant. He said his uncle drives the vehicle, but his uncle was not in it at the time. Asked about his driving licence, Saju said he had a licence for light vehicles.

After Saju left, a filling station official and several local people approached me and asked what I was working on. One of them described how drivers collect less fuel than their allocated amount but take the full amount of money. While standing at the filling station, I phoned the assigned driver, Sardar Humayun Kabir, several times on his mobile phone. He did not answer. As a result, I could not obtain his explanation at the time for allowing someone else to drive the vehicle.

A local later said that vehicles began arriving at the filling station again about half an hour after I left that night. Asked whether Humayun Kabir held any position in the union, its president Shah Alam Talukder said he was not on the committee.

However, he said Kabir was close to him and often stayed with him. When questioned about allowing others to drive the vehicles, the union president spoke about the long hours drivers have to work. He claimed that drivers sometimes have to work 15 to 17 hours. However, DSCC sources said drivers operate vehicles for seven to eight hours in total, covering both day and night shifts.

At around 10:30 pm the following day, 5 October, I went to another garage where the corporation parks its vehicles, beside the Sayedabad bus terminal. The site, near the railway line leading towards the Padma Bridge, previously housed Wonderland Park. Vehicles were leaving the garage one after another to collect waste. However, two vehicles bearing registration numbers 11-4270 and 11-4307 were not leaving.

These two vehicles were among those identified in the investigation as being driven by people other than their assigned drivers. I stayed there for about an hour and a half. At one point, news of a journalist's presence spread, and at least 35 drivers gathered around me to ask what I was investigating. Eventually, I left following the intervention of a senior corporation official. I could not speak to the drivers of the two vehicles that day.

The driver of another vehicle, bearing registration number 11-4278, could not be located the previous night either. The vehicle remained parked beside the Sayedabad bus terminal from 11:00 pm on 4 October to 2:30 am on 5 October. Earlier information had also indicated that this vehicle was being driven by people other than its assigned driver. Despite waiting for a long time, I could not locate the driver to verify his identity that night.

Others also take the driver's seat amid driver shortage

DSCC has a total of 608 vehicles and pieces of equipment, including excavators, road rollers and bulldozers. Against this, it has 252 permanent drivers. This figure includes not only waste transport vehicles but also other vehicles and equipment owned by the corporation. To address the shortage of drivers, employees in other positions, including cleaners and mosquito control workers, are also assigned driving duties.

Union President Shah Alam Talukder confirmed that the corporation has 252 permanent drivers. According to him, employees in other positions who have driving licences and the necessary skills are assigned driving duties after being tested by officials.

However, the investigation found that in the cases of the vehicles identified, the assigned drivers themselves were allowing others to drive them at their own discretion. Officials concerned said many obtain such opportunities through arrangements with transport workers' leaders.

Regarding the shortage of drivers, Administrator Abdus Salam said he had recruited some drivers after taking charge and that more would be recruited. Proposals outlining staffing requirements in different departments had been sent to the ministry. However, he said the corporation also had to consider its ability to pay salaries before increasing its workforce.

Allocated fuel sold at the filling station

Household waste from the 75 DSCC wards is first brought to secondary transfer stations (STSs). From there, it is transported by vehicles to the Matuail landfill. A total of 237 vehicles and pieces of equipment are used for waste transportation and landfill management. These include both waste transport vehicles and equipment used at the landfill.

Vehicles with capacities of 3, 5, 10, 15 and 20 tonnes are used to transport waste. Sources concerned said these vehicles travel between the STSs and Matuail three to four times every night. However, union president Shah Alam Talukder claimed that at least four trips are required to clear the waste, while some vehicles make as many as five trips.

According to sources concerned, the fuel allocation ranges from eight to 14 litres per trip, depending on the vehicle and route. There are allegations that fuel is siphoned off by taking advantage of allocations that are three to four litres higher per trip than necessary. Instead of filling the vehicles with the entire allocated amount, the remaining fuel is sold at a lower price at the filling station. An official working at the pump told Prothom Alo, on condition of anonymity, that everyone knows DSCC drivers sell some of their allocated fuel at a slightly lower price. There is nothing to hide about it.

At the municipal filling station, this correspondent spoke to a local man. Describing the transactions, he said that if 12 litres of fuel were allocated for a trip, the driver would take only eight or nine litres. The money for the remaining fuel would be kept on account. Pump employees record the transactions in writing, and the money is handed over to the assigned driver around the middle or at the end of the month. According to his account, even when someone else drives a vehicle, the financial records remain under the name of its assigned driver.

Sources concerned alleged that some drivers, union leaders and officials concerned receive shares of this money. However, no details could be obtained about how much money each person received.

Shah Alam Talukder, president of the Transport Drivers, Workers and Employees Union, denied allegations that he received commissions from fuel sales. He said he was employed, received a salary and lived on that income. He said he did not have specific records of how much fuel each vehicle consumed.

According to him, the engines of some vehicles have to remain running to operate their hydraulic systems. Therefore, fuel consumption cannot be calculated uniformly for all vehicles based solely on the distance travelled.

According to estimates by sources concerned, an average of 5,842 trips are made every month. If three litres of fuel are siphoned off per trip, the total amounts to 17,526 litres a month. At the government's October retail price of Tk 135 per litre, the market value of this diesel stands at Tk 2.37 million. If the practice continues at the same rate for a year and prices remain unchanged, the amount would be approximately Tk 28.4 million.

Regarding allegations of fuel sales and the protection provided by union leaders, DSCC Administrator Abdus Salam said forming trade unions is a workers' right and he could not curtail that right. However, he said he would investigate if specific allegations were brought to his attention. If anyone's involvement is proven, various disciplinary measures, including dismissal from service, would be taken.

Deaths, suspensions, yet same irregularities persist

On 24 November 2021, Notre Dame College student Naim Hasan was run over by a DSCC garbage transport truck while crossing the road in Gulistan. The following day, police said the vehicle was being driven by Russell Khan, who was not a regular employee of the corporation and did not have a driving licence. According to the police, he had become involved in cleaning work through a relative and subsequently got the opportunity to drive the vehicle.

The corporation's investigation into the incident uncovered several stages through which responsibility for the vehicle had changed hands. The vehicle was assigned to Iran Mia. It was handed over to Harun from the transport pool, and Harun then allowed Russell to drive it. In other words, the keys passed through several hands from the driver officially listed in the records before reaching an unlicensed person.

Following Naim's death, students staged protests in Gulistan. On 25 November, they surrounded Nagar Bhaban, demanding justice and safer roads. The then DSCC mayor, Sheikh Fazle Noor Taposh, came out and addressed them. In December 2022, police submitted a charge sheet to the court against three people in the case filed by Naim's father. Those accused included suspended driver Iran Mia, Harun and Russell. An arrest warrant was also issued against Iran Mia at the time.

However, despite the filing of cases and investigations into these incidents, the families have yet to receive justice. Asked about the matter, Naim Hasan's father, Shah Alam Dewan, told Prothom Alo over the phone yesterday, Friday, “Everything ended after the case was filed. No one followed up afterwards. I struggled so hard to get my son into Notre Dame College, but everything came to an end.”

Expressing his frustration, he said, “A culture of impunity has persisted for many years. What more can I say about it!”

On 8 December 2021, nine drivers were suspended following Naim's death. The allegation was that they had allowed others to drive the vehicles assigned to them instead of driving them themselves. Seven of them were garbage truck drivers and two drove light vehicles. Transport Supervisor Faruk Ahmed was also dismissed over allegations that he had allowed someone else to drive a vehicle assigned to another person. However, he was later reinstated.

About two and a half years later, on 25 April 2024, Mahin Ahmed, a seventh gradef at Motijheel Ideal School, was killed after being hit by a garbage truck in Medinabagh, Mugda. According to a corporation order, Kamal, the driver of vehicle number 11-4281, had assigned Rubel to drive it instead of driving it himself. Neither the driver nor the two cleaners assigned to the vehicle were present in it at the time of the accident. All three were dismissed for negligence of duty.

On 23 October 2025, laundry shop employee Iqbal Hossain was killed in Kalapatty, Jatrabari. A garbage truck hit him while he was returning home after work. According to police, the vehicle was being driven by the driver's assistant. He was detained and the vehicle was seized. Naim, followed by Mahin and then Iqbal — in all three cases, someone other than the assigned driver was behind the wheel.

At least 18 deaths in 9 years

According to accident records uncovered by the investigation, two people named Rimon and Sharin were killed after being run over by a garbage truck in front of the Basabo Buddhist Temple in September 2017. Two more people died in two separate accidents in 2018. Badsha Mia was killed at Dainik Bangla intersection on 12 May, while motorcyclist Nurjahan Pushan died in Bakshibazar on 23 November. Her husband was also injured.

Information was found on six incidents in 2021 in which six people died. Khalid, an employee of the state-run Bangladesh Sangbad Sangstha (BSS), was killed in Dayaganj on 20 January; rickshaw puller Mostafa died in Jatrabari on 16 April; and bank employee Swapan Ahmed Dipu was killed in Titipara in May. Garment worker Faruk Hossain died in Dolaipar on the night of 9 August. Naim was killed on 24 November, followed by Swapan Kumar Sarkar in Wari on 23 December.

Nasrin Khanam was killed in Khilgaon on 1 April 2022, and Nazma Begum died in Titipara on 31 May. On 5 August 2023, another woman, Nazma Begum, was killed in the Bhanga Press area of Jatrabari. At the time, the corporation denied that its vehicle was involved in the incident. However, a subsequent investigation confirmed that the vehicle belonged to Dhaka South City Corporation.

Following Mahin's death in 2024, three people were killed in two separate incidents in 2025. Besides Iqbal, university students Gazi Iram Ridwan and Tahsin Tapu were killed in Demra on 12 December. On 4 April this year, businessman Sajedul Islam lost his life in South Banasree. By this count, 18 people have been killed in 16 accidents since 2017.

Regarding the accidents, DSCC Administrator Abdus Salam said that following an accident after he took charge, he instructed officials not to allow anyone without a driving licence to operate the vehicles. He claimed that no such incident had occurred since the instruction was issued.

When informed about the incident at the municipal filling station involving a relative of the assigned driver, he asked for the specific details to be submitted to him. He said he would take disciplinary action if the information was provided.

Asked why officials were not supervising the drivers, the administrator said it was not possible to make sweeping statements about incidents that had not come to his attention.

The DSCC added that action would also be taken against officials responsible for supervising the drivers if they allowed others to operate the vehicles in this way.

City corporation must take responsibility

Former BUET professor and transport expert Shamsul Haque told Prothom Alo that although city corporation administrators are currently taking various bold initiatives, an unbiased approach is essential in this regard. Before disciplining or controlling others, they must first put their own house in order; otherwise, such efforts amount to nothing more than an assertion of authority.

He questioned whether the city corporation's garbage trucks were actually roadworthy, whether their drivers held valid licences and whether people other than the authorised drivers were operating the vehicles.

He said the city corporation itself must bear the primary responsibility for the deaths of ordinary people caused by its garbage trucks, rather than holding only the drivers accountable. Sustainable solutions will be possible only when reforms begin within the organisation itself, and the initiatives taken will then earn public trust.

item.title: PM visits hospitals, educational institutions to assess dengue situation
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Saturday morning began visiting hospitals and educational institutions in the capital to assess the dengue situation and cleanliness activities.
The prime minister left his Gulshan residence at 9:10am for the surprise visits, his Deputy Press Secretary Hasan Shiplu said.
He said Tarique Rahman first went to Kuwait-Bangladesh Friendship Government Hospital in Uttara to see firsthand the measures taken by the hospital authorities to tackle dengue.
He then visited Rajuk Uttara Model College, where he addressed members of the Bangladesh National Cadet Corps (BNCC), urging them to play an active role in cleanliness drives to help prevent dengue.
The prime minister will also visit Dhaka Medical College Hospital and various hospitals under Dhaka North and South city corporations, Shiplu said.
On September 12, the prime minister launched a three-month special campaign to prevent dengue, featuring cleanliness drives and public awareness activities.
Considering the next three months a high-risk period for dengue, he urged people across the country to actively participate in the campaign.

item.title: Five killed in fire at Cox’s Bazar resort
item.description:
At least five people have died in a fire at Tup-Tup Resort in the Patuartek area near Inani Beach in Ukhia upazila of Cox’s Bazar.
The fire broke out around 7am on Saturday at the resort along Marine Drive. Fire Service officials and police have warned that the death toll could rise.
Senior Fire Service official Dolan Acharya confirmed that five bodies had been recovered. The victims are believed to be tourists, but their identities could not be immediately established.
Ukhia police station Officer-in-Charge Atiqur Rahman said the death toll might increase as rescue workers continued searching the site. Police are working to establish the victims’ identities and determine the total number of casualties.
According to the fire service, three firefighting units reached the scene around 8am and began operations. The blaze was brought under control around 10am, after which rescuers began searching the resort.
The resort, built primarily of wood, sustained extensive damage. Firefighters are continuing to search the building for anyone who may remain trapped inside.
Local residents said the resort’s staff and management left the scene after the fire broke out.
The cause of the fire, the extent of the damage and whether the resort had adequate fire safety measures remain unclear.

item.title: A card is not a safety net if the poor remain invisible
item.description:
A garment worker loses her job. A riverbank family is displaced. A widow suddenly becomes the sole provider for her children. Their circumstances can change overnight; a government beneficiary list may not.
That time lag is not just a clerical inconvenience. For a household already choosing between food and medicine, a temporary hardship can turn into lasting poverty.
This is why Bangladesh's latest social protection exercise deserves more scrutiny than the excitement surrounding a new card.
On October 12, the government began nationwide door-to-door collection of household information for the Family Card program. Officials say the database is intended to cover approximately 45 million households, with data collection due to conclude on November 30.
It is an ambitious administrative undertaking. But its success will depend less on the number of entries gathered than on the number of vulnerable families no longer falling through the cracks.
The World Bank's October 2026 Bangladesh Development update offers a sobering benchmark. It estimates that the number of people living in poverty increased by approximately 2.1 million in FY2025-26, while about half of the poorest households remain outside social protection programs.
These findings should be read together. At precisely the moment when more families need a cushion, the existing system struggles to reach many who are already at the bottom.
For too long, our public conversation has treated social protection as a contest of allocations: How many schemes, how many beneficiaries, how many billions of taka. Those figures matter, but they cannot establish whether assistance is timely, adequate, or fairly targeted.
A benefit announced is not necessarily a benefit received; a name on a list is not an assurance of future eligibility; and a card in a wallet does not, by itself, protect a family against the next shock.
The central policy challenge is what economists call exclusion error: Households that qualify for assistance are left out.
At the same time, inclusion errors can direct scarce resources to those who do not qualify. Perfect targeting is impossible, but both forms of error can be measured and reduced.
The new exercise relies on a proxy means test to estimate household welfare from observable characteristics. That is more systematic than selection by discretion alone, yet a score cannot fully capture a sudden dismissal, an expensive illness, or the loss of land to a river. A statistical estimate should guide an eligibility decision, not make it immune to challenge.
An announced benefit is not necessarily a benefit received; a card in a wallet is not protection against the next shock.
The government's stated plan to receive appeals online and through union parishad service centres is therefore important. But an appeal mechanism is meaningful only if it works for people with limited literacy, poor connectivity, or no local influence.
Applicants should receive intelligible reasons for rejection, a tracking number, and a decision within a published period. Independent spot checks and public reporting on overturned decisions could separate a functioning grievance system from a mere box for collecting complaints.
Even a carefully constructed database can become obsolete. A household above the eligibility threshold today may fall below it after an illness, a price shock, or river erosion.
Bangladesh needs its planned dynamic social registry to work as a continuously updated public service, rather than a one-off enumeration exercise.
Households must be able to report changes without incurring expensive travel or relying on unofficial intermediaries. In disaster-affected localities, rapid reassessments should be possible without waiting for another nationwide survey.
This matters particularly in the informal economy, where fluctuating earnings rarely appear in conventional employment records.
Program design poses a second challenge. Issuing the Family Card in a woman's name is a potentially valuable recognition of her economic agency. Yet, deprivation is not identical for every member of a household.
An older person requiring care, a person with a disability, and a child facing malnutrition need different combinations of services. Integrating databases and eliminating unnecessary duplication are sensible objectives.
Replacing every specialized program with an undifferentiated household payment would not be sensible. The goal should be a common gateway to appropriately tailored support.
Privacy must be treated as a condition of inclusion, not an afterthought. A registry on this scale will contain sensitive information about identities, assets, and family circumstances. Without safeguards, it could expose vulnerable people to data misuse or unjust exclusion.
Information collection should be proportionate to need, access restricted to official roles, changes auditable, and errors correctable by the households concerned. Program performance should be transparent; recipients' private circumstances should not be.
There will be a familiar objection: Bangladesh cannot afford administrative perfection while its budget is under strain. The fiscal constraint is real.
According to the World Bank, revenue collection stood at only 8.3% of GDP in FY2025-26, and economic growth is projected at 3.4% in FY2026-27. Yet scarcity strengthens the case for accuracy.
Every avoidable duplicate payment, unresolved exclusion, or delayed transfer carries a higher social cost when the fiscal room for correction is so narrow. Better targeting is not a substitute for adequate funding; it is a way to improve the impact of that funding.
Indeed, the World Bank estimates that, under a reform scenario combining better-targeted existing cash programs, food-subsidy consolidation, and the Family Card, an additional 2.85 million people could be lifted out of poverty, and this is a modelled possibility, not an assured outcome.
It nevertheless illustrates why the quality of implementation matters. Nor should the reform agenda be reduced to austerity. Removing subsidies before dependable compensation reaches vulnerable households would shift the burden of adjustment onto those least able to bear it.
A credible reform program should publish a modest set of results every quarter: The share of the poorest households receiving assistance, the time between approval and first payment, the proportion of grievances resolved, payment failure rates, and whether women can access transfers without intermediaries.
District-level comparisons, with appropriate privacy safeguards, would help locate persistent gaps. An independent evaluation after the first year would reveal far more than a ceremony celebrating cards distributed.
Ultimately, social protection is about the relationship between citizens and the state. A fair system does not require a family to prove its desperation repeatedly or to rely on familiarity with an official. It recognizes vulnerability, responds when circumstances change, and explains decisions that affect people's lives.
Bangladesh has an opportunity to make the Family Card more than another symbol of welfare reform. The next milestone should not simply be the completion of a national database. It should be the moment when an eligible household can trust that need, rather than connections or procedural luck, determines access to assistance.
A safety net earns its name not when a card is issued, but when someone falling is actually caught.
Dr Munshi Muhammad Abdul Kader Jilani holds a PhD in Knowledge Management from Wuhan University of Technology in China. He is currently working as an Assistant Professor at the Bangladesh Institute of Governance and Management (BIGM), University of Dhaka (Affiliated), and Associate Editor of the BIGM Journal of Policy Analysis.

item.title: Memory as identity, memory as a file cabinet
item.description:
Recently, we lost a dear family friend who lived to the remarkable age of 100 years and 9 months. She attended our wedding back in the late 1970s, and we remained in touch over the years.
During the last two decades especially, we visited her frequently in Paris. Now that she is gone, our memories of her live on, providing us with a source of comfort and contentment, and serving as a kind of shock absorber as we come to terms with her loss.
She lived in Bangladesh as a UN official, and had contributed to the women’s developmental issues in the mid-1970s. Bangladesh had a special place in her heart. She would always read my pieces -- even after she turned 100 -- and share her comments when we called her for long chats. I always found her feedback thoughtful and uplifting.
She would also advise me to read something she discovered. Decades ago, she introduced me to the works of philosopher Rene Girard (1923-2015) -- almost her namesake; ours was Renee Gerard (1926-2026).
Remembering her company, advice, chats in her book-filled living room in Paris, or having a meal at a Parisian restaurant gave me the idea of writing on memories. Suddenly, I remembered what our English teacher KPC (Kali Prashad Chaterjee) at Bagerhat High School taught us when elucidating William Wordsworth’s poem The Daffodils. KPC, summarizing the poem, told us that you find joy twice: First, by seeing the daffodils in the lake, and then again by remembering them.
This is what human memory does. It is not an archive we consult but a place we return to -- and we come back changed, often with a smile on our face.
Imagine life without memory. Each moment would arrive without a past and depart without a future to hold it. We could still eat, work, and move through the day, but nothing would add up.
A life lived only in the now is a series of disjointed events, not a story. It is memory that turns events into a biography, and a biography into an identity. We know who we are because we remember who we have been, and whom we have been with.
Nowhere is this clearer than in grief. When someone we love dies, what remains is not a file but a relationship that continues inside us. I remember my mother's laughter while reading Shibram Chakraborty, or Syed Mujtaba Ali. I remember a teacher's scolding, or a rare, hard-won praise.
These memories hurt, yet they also hold us. They remind us that we were loved, that we belonged somewhere, that someone's life was woven into ours.
Mourning is, in large part, the slow work of converting an absence into a memory we can live with. The dead do not leave us entirely so long as we remember them, and in remembering them we remember ourselves.
Memory also gives us a sense of direction. We recall the choices that led us here, the sacrifices others made, the values we were handed and the ones we chose. From these we draw purpose. A person who remembers a parent's quiet persistence may find the strength to persist. A person who remembers a friend's generosity may decide to be generous.
Human memory is also practical. We use it to solve problems, to recall what Marx said and where -- “peasants are like potatoes in a sack” in the Eighteenth Brumaire -- as students remain impressed. Memory helps us learn, plan, and function. In this respect, it resembles the memory of a computer, which also stores information and retrieves it when needed.
The comparison is tempting, and it is useful as far as it goes. Both kinds of memory help a system get things done.
But the parallel ends there. A computer's memory is functional through and through. It stores data in order to process it, and it retrieves data in order to complete a task. When a hard drive holds 10,000 photographs, none of them is more precious than another unless a program is told to rank them. Nothing in the machine aches when a file is deleted. Nothing is consoled when a file is restored. The memory serves the operation and has no stake in what it holds.
The newest AI systems, for all their astonishing fluency, do not change this. They can recall vast amounts of information, summarize a life, even write a convincing elegy. They can store and retrieve what we tell them about our parents.
Yet storing is not remembering.
There is, as far as we can tell, no one inside who is comforted by the retrieval, no one for whom the stored detail is a loss or a gift. These systems generate words about meaning without, so far as we know, experiencing meaning.
Their memory is a tool. Ours is a part of who we are.
There is a quiet lesson here about how we live: If memory is where meaning is made, then we have a responsibility to tend to it. We can ask our elders for their stories before it is too late. We can name the people who shaped us and tell their stories to the young. We can resist the thin, hurried present in which nothing is remembered because nothing is allowed to matter.
A culture that stops remembering together -- in rituals, anniversaries, and family tables -- will find that it has plenty of data and very little meaning.
At its core, computer memory is a vast digital filing system built on billions of microscopic electronic switches called transistors, but it has no emotion, least consciousness. Its functional power lies in speed and exact replication: It can store billions of these tiny data points, execute complex calculations, and retrieve files with absolute precision in nanoseconds without ever degrading, misremembering, or imbuing a single byte with emotion.
Computers will keep getting better at storing everything. What they cannot do, at least for now, is care about what they store.
That is our work, and also our gift. We remember -- not only to function, but to belong, to grieve, to love, and to go on.
Habibul Haque Khondker is a sociologist and columnist.

item.title: Doing all we can to reduce poverty
item.description:
As the world observed the International Day for Eradication of Poverty, it is clear that our national reflections must be anchored in sobering reality rather than complacent rhetoric.
The World Bank’s latest revelations -- confirming that our GDP growth has slumped to a dismal 3.4% and that over 2 million additional people have been pushed into poverty over the past year -- expose what must be identified as a profound socio-economic crisis.
For a nation that long aspired towards double digit growth, to have been reduced to below 4% for consecutive years is a significant blow. We must also contend with the fact that nearly 62 million citizens live just above the poverty line, meaning a single health shock, price spike, or market disruption can plunge entire families back into extreme hardship.
To that end, poverty eradication remains a distant dream for our country, and that is the reality. However, addressing it, and ensuring that we pull people out of poverty every day instead, is an urgent national emergency.
For too long, our poverty alleviation strategies have relied on fragmented, leaky safety programs that frequently miss the poorest segments of society while misallocating resources. While we are looking to change that narrative with the Family Card program, we must ensure that we get this right.
It goes without saying that a nation striving for structural reform can no longer tolerate a system where wealth inequality widens while the vulnerable absorb the harshest blows of economic stagnation.
Reducing poverty must go beyond merely managing destitution for our population. While the short term requires us to pull more and more people out of extreme poverty, the end goal must be to fix our macroeconomic foundations, drive job creation, and ensure that economic recovery lifts every citizen, not just a privileged few.
The end goal must always be to become an equitable nation, not merely a prosperous one.

item.title: Dhaka's air quality remains 'unhealthy'
item.description:
The air quality in Dhaka remained unhealthy on Saturday morning, with an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 166 at 9:14am.
With this score, the capital ranked ninth among the world's most polluted cities.
Iraq’s Baghdad, Singapore’s Singapore, Pakistan’s Lahore and India’s Mumbai occupied the top four spots on the list, with AQI scores of 378, 206, 201 and 192, respectively.
An AQI score between 50 and 100 is considered "moderate" with an acceptable air quality, while one between 101 and 150 is considered "unhealthy for sensitive groups", while a score between 151 and 200 is classified as "unhealthy."
AQI readings between 201 and 300 are termed "very unhealthy", and anything above 301 is considered "hazardous", posing serious health risks.
The AQI provides daily updates on air quality, indicating how clean or polluted the air is and highlighting potential health impacts.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with air pollution, with air quality typically deteriorating during winter and improving during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution causes around seven million deaths globally each year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

item.title: Former additional secretary found dead at Officers Club
item.description:
The body of former additional secretary Md Mosharraf Hossain was recovered from a building under construction at the Officers Club in Dhaka’s Ramna area on Friday morning.
Police recovered the body around 11:45am.
Mosharraf Hossain, a member of the Officers Club, lived with his family in Banani.
According to reports, he arrived at the club around 10am with his youngest daughter. He left her near the swimming pool, beside the building under construction, and entered the structure.
About an hour later, his body was found in a bloodied condition on the ground floor near a staircase.
Sheikh Zahidul Islam, deputy commissioner of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police’s Ramna division, said Mosharraf had poor eyesight and apparently fell from the third floor into an open space on the ground floor.
“We have completed the preliminary examination of the body,” he said.
The deputy commissioner said the family had requested that no post-mortem examination be conducted and that the body would be handed over to them.
Mosharraf’s eldest daughter lives in the United States. According to the family, his burial will take place after she arrives in Bangladesh.

item.title: Man Utd have 'moved on' from Martinez outburst, says Carrick
item.description:
Michael Carrick said Friday that Manchester United had "moved on" from Lisandro Martinez's outburst aimed at the club's hierarchy, stressing it was "really not a drama for us as a group".
Argentina defender Martinez took aim at the United hierarchy following their 2-0 Champions League loss to Atletico Madrid on Tuesday, saying Carrick had been left with an under-strength squad.
The centre-back criticised technical director Jason Wilcox, saying he had "100 percent" expected more investment during the summer transfer window after United finished third in the Premier League last season.
It is understood Martinez, who issued an apology on Thursday, has been fined for his outburst.
United manager Carrick confirmed during a pre-match press conference on Friday that Martinez would be in his squad for their Premier League match at bitter rivals Leeds on Sunday.
Carrick, under intense pressure after a terrible start to the season, was asked by reporters about Martinez's comments and subsequent developments.
"We've moved on from that, it was one of those things," he said. "I think Licha (Martinez) has come out and acknowledged the situation and as a group we've moved on.
"It's really not a drama for us as a group, I think the boys have trained really well. This morning there was a really good feeling around the squad."
Martinez, 28, said in a statement he had held positive talks with the club's leadership and Carrick.
"Everyone knows that I am a passionate person and that I live football with great intensity," he said in a post on Instagram.
"The frustration of the defeat led me to express how I felt at a time and place that perhaps were not the right ones, and for that I want to apologise."
- 'Emotion' -
Former United captain Roy Keane has branded the situation at his former club "a bit of a circus".
Carrick was pressed by reporters on the nature of the apology from Martinez, which did not mention Wilcox by name.
"I think he (Martinez) has released his statement and he's realised he's made a mistake," said the United boss. "I think that's enough for all of us to move on with."
He added: "I understand the emotion at times. We ask for passion, we ask for emotion, we ask for fire and we ask for players to care.
"There's a way of doing that and that's already been acknowledged. We need to carry that. We need to carry that intensity and that willingness and that togetherness and that spirit and everything."
United have made their worst start to a league season in 40 years.
They are 13th in the Premier League, with just one win from six matches, but Carrick, a former United and England midfielder, deflected a question about the pressure on him personally.
"I don't need results, we all need results," he said. "It's not about me. Manchester United is a lot bigger than any individual, bigger than me.
"Bigger than any player, anyone else who works at this football club. It always has been, and it's not about me."

item.title: Mohammedan, Kings clinch BFL victories
item.description:
Mohammedan Sporting Club continued their winning run in the Bangladesh Football League with a 2–0 victory over PWD Sports Club, while Bashundhara Kings registered a comfortable 3–0 win over City Club on Friday.
At Shaheed Miraj-Tapan Stadium in Manikganj, Mohammedan secured their third consecutive victory thanks to goals from Malian forward Souleymane Diabate and midfielder Minhazul Abedin Rakib.
Diabate broke the deadlock soon after the break, scoring in the 47th minute to put the traditional Motijheel outfit ahead.
Rakib then sealed the victory with the second goal in the 78th minute, ensuring Mohammedan collected all three points.
PWD attempted to fight back but failed to find the net as Mohammedan maintained their winning momentum.
The victory took Mohammedan to nine points from three matches, while PWD remained on three points after four outings.
Meanwhile, Bashundhara Kings returned to winning ways with a 3–0 victory over City Club at Shaheed Barkat Stadium in Gazipur.
Brazilian forward Robson Azevedo da Silva took the lead in the 49th minute. Nigerian forward Chukwuiebube Emeka Ogbugh doubled the lead from the penalty spot in the 72nd minute.
Midfielder Sayed Shah Quazem Kirmanee completed the rout with a third goal four minutes into the stoppage time.
The victory was Kings’ second in the league, taking their tally to seven points from three matches. City Club also have seven points but have played four matches.
In Saturday’s fourth-round fixtures, Abahani Limited, Dhaka, will take on Chattogram City Football Club at Mymensingh District Stadium.
Rahmatganj Muslim Friends Society will face Brothers Union at Birshreshtha Flight Lieutenant Matiur Rahman Stadium in Munshiganj, while Bangladesh Police Football Club will meet Arambagh Krira Sangha at Shaheed Barkat Stadium in Gazipur.

item.title: Ending the culture of violence against journalists
item.description:
The killing of a journalist in Netrokona is another grim reminder of the dangers faced by those who investigate wrongdoing and bring uncomfortable truths to public attention.
Such attacks carry consequences that extend far beyond the individual victim: They threaten the public’s right to information and undermine the very foundations of accountability.
Lutfuzzaman Alif Fakir, a Netrokona correspondent for Ruposhi Bangla who frequently reported on corruption through his page Detective Article, was shot dead by unidentified assailants in Durgapur on Thursday night. He had previously survived a violent attack in November of last year.
This tragedy raises serious questions about whether adequate protective measures were taken following that prior incident.
It must be made clear: This culture of violence against journalists is completely unacceptable and must be brought under control.
The authorities must treat this killing with the urgency it demands. The perpetrators must be identified, arrested, and brought to justice through a prompt and transparent investigation.
Without accountability, those who resort to violence to silence the press will only feel emboldened.
However, seeking justice after a killing is not enough. Bangladesh urgently needs a proactive system to safeguard journalists before threats escalate into tragedy.
Complaints of intimidation and physical violence must be investigated immediately, backed by credible risk assessments and timely protection. Local law enforcement must take threats against reporters seriously -- especially when victims have already experienced violence.
Media organizations also share a duty to establish safety protocols, provide legal assistance, and stand by journalists facing danger due to their work. Freelancers and local correspondents, who often operate with limited institutional support, must not be left behind.
A free press cannot function when journalists are forced to choose between speaking the truth and preserving their lives. Nor can citizens expect corruption and abuse of power to be exposed if those who investigate them are left exposed to harm.
This tragedy must spur concrete action. Protecting journalists is nothing less than protecting democracy itself.

item.title: Strikes hit airport complex in Yemen's govt-held Aden, Houthis claim attack
item.description:
Two missiles landed Friday within the perimeter of the airport in the Yemeni city of Aden, the interim capital of the Saudi-backed government, authorities said, with the Houthis claiming the attack.
The Houthis are fighting both Yemen's internationally recognised government and their Saudi allies.
In a statement attributed to a military source, the Houthis said an attack targeted "the Saudi forces' command headquarters in the Badr camp in Aden province" as well as a weapons depot.
An AFP journalist heard two loud explosions from the vicinity of the airport, but was not in a position to confirm what precisely had been hit.
The Yemeni information ministry said in a statement that a Yemenia Airways flight from Aden to Cairo narrowly missed being struck.
It was "preparing for takeoff at the very moment when the terrorist Houthi militia targeted the airport with two missiles that landed approximately 500 metres from the aircraft and about 100 metres from the centre of the runway," a statement said.
"What occurred was not merely an assault on a civilian airport, but a direct threat to the lives of passengers and flight crews, to aviation safety, and a grave violation of international laws and norms."
The Aden Capital Security Department said in a statement "that two rockets launched by the Houthi movement landed inside the Aden International Airport complex, in the second incident of its kind in less than a week".
"According to preliminary information, no loss of life was recorded as a result of the incident."
