item.title: Fire breaks out at Cox’s Bazar resort, 10 dead, 6 victims identified
item.description:
The death toll from a fire at a wooden resort on Patuartek Sea Beach in Inani, Ukhiya, Cox’s Bazar, has risen to 10.

The fire broke out at around 7:30am today, Saturday.

At 2:15pm today, Cox’s Bazar Fire Service Assistant Deputy Director Syed Morshed Hossain confirmed to Prothom Alo that 10 bodies had been recovered.

He said there might be more bodies and that the rescue operation was underway.

Fire breaks out at Cox’s Bazar resort, six bodies recovered, six injured, all victims tourists

Six of the 10 victims have been identified. They are Israt Jahan Maliha (30) and Milita Mehezabin Alvi (23) of Banasree in Dhaka; Laila Jahan Nabila (27) and Nafista Mim (27) of Khilgaon; Fariha Kabir (33) of Chuadanga; and five-year-old Faizan Ahmed.

Cox’s Bazar Sadar Hospital Resident Medical Officer (RMO) Subaktagin Mahmud Sohel confirmed their identities.

Ukhiya Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) Panna Akter told Prothom Alo that the identities of the four bodies recovered later could not be confirmed as they had been badly burnt. Their identities will be confirmed through DNA tests.

Six people who suffered burns in the fire are receiving treatment at Cox’s Bazar Sadar Hospital. They are Mugda Medical College Hospital physician Shihab Uddin (31), his wife Nafiza Newaz Khan (29), Mannan (34), Meherunnesa (30), Masud (30) and Samida (32).

Locals said the fire broke out at the resort, located beside Marine Drive, at around 7:30am. On receiving the news, firefighters arrived at the scene. Later, locals, with police assistance, began efforts to bring the fire under control and rescue people.

A visit to the scene found firefighters continuing rescue operations, while police were also present. The cause of the fire was not immediately known.

Cox’s Bazar Deputy Commissioner Md A Mannan told Prothom Alo that the fire was suspected to have originated from the stove in the resort's kitchen.

A five-member investigation committee, headed by the Additional District Magistrate, has been formed to investigate the cause of the fire, he added.

item.title: Why are people struggling in a country with a per capita income of 3000 dollars?
item.description:
On paper, Bangladesh is now a country with a per capita income of $3,000. But to a housewife standing with a shopping bag in hand at the market, or a construction worker counting his wages at the end of the day, this figure means little.

They are doing a different calculation: expenses are rising faster than income. It is a topsy-turvy game. Per capita income rises, yet the number of poor people increases; economic growth stalls, but the state’s debt keeps growing.

According to preliminary estimates by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS), per capita income reached $3,020 for the first time in fiscal year 2025–26. However, that estimate was based on an assumed growth rate of 4.14 per cent. In the revised estimate, growth has fallen to 3.68 per cent.
The World Bank’s latest forecast suggests that economic growth may remain stuck at around 3.4 per cent in the current fiscal year as well. The record in average income, therefore, does not translate into a record in ordinary people’s purchasing power.

The clearest evidence of this is found in the poverty figures. According to the 2016 Household Income and Expenditure Survey, the poverty rate stood at 24.3 per cent. By 2022, it had fallen to 18.7 per cent—one of the most significant achievements in a decade and a half.

However, a newly published World Bank report says that the national poverty rate has risen for four consecutive years, reaching an estimated 22.5 per cent in 2026. At the international poverty line of $3 a day, nearly 2.1 million people fell into poverty in the last fiscal year alone.
In other words, in just four years, we have come close to losing much of the progress achieved over an entire decade. Yet 62 per cent of the country’s poor still remain outside the social safety net.

At the heart of this reversal in poverty reduction lies a shortage of jobs. According to the full report of the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics’ Labour Force Survey, the country has 2.624 million unemployed people, of whom 2.032 million are young people aged 15 to 29.

In other words, three out of every four unemployed people are young. Nearly 885,000 unemployed people have higher education qualifications. Women’s participation in the labour force has also fallen, from 42.8 per cent in 2022 to 38.4 per cent.

The situation in the industrial sector is even more worrying. According to Industrial Police data, 457 industrial factories shut down permanently in the two years between June 2024 and June 2026, including 170 in the textile and garment sectors.

According to entrepreneurs’ associations, the number exceeds 500. In the garment sector alone, around 150,000 workers have lost their jobs. The reasons are multifaceted, including shortages of gas and electricity, a decline in work orders, complications involving loans and letters of credit (LCs), and labour unrest.

The pressure of rising prices has compounded the jobs crisis. Inflation stood at 8.34 per cent in September, while wages increased by just 7.90 per cent. The outlook ahead offers little relief either. The International Monetary Fund’s October 2026 World Economic Outlook projects that average inflation could rise to 10.9 per cent in the current 2026–27 fiscal year, while GDP growth could fall to 3.2 per cent. If this forecast proves accurate, it would be the lowest growth rate in nearly four decades.

Meanwhile, rising global oil prices due to the war in the Middle East have prompted the government to adjust fuel prices three times in seven months. Since September 21, diesel has cost Tk 135 per litre, kerosene Tk 155, petrol Tk 160 and octane Tk 165, the highest prices in the country’s history. In June, retail electricity prices rose by an average of 16.68 per cent to Tk 10.63 per unit. The price of a 12-kilogram LPG cylinder also increased in October.

The government argues that although prices in the global market have more than doubled, domestic prices have not been adjusted fully. Even so, the Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation (BPC) incurred losses of approximately Tk 22,876 crore between March and August. This argument is not without merit.

However, higher fuel costs feed through irrigation and transportation expenses, ultimately pushing up the prices of rice, lentils, vegetables and fish. Working people cope with the shock by putting less food on their plates, dipping into their savings and borrowing money.

The deepest wound in the economy, however, lies in the banking sector. At the end of June 2026, defaulted loans stood at Tk 606,555 crore, accounting for 32.78 per cent of all outstanding loans. With such an enormous amount of money tied up in defaulted loans, banks are unable to lend to new entrepreneurs. This is also a major reason why private-sector credit growth has fallen below 5 per cent.

Meanwhile, the government’s debt burden continues to grow. According to the Finance Division, in June 2024, at the end of the previous government’s tenure and before the July mass uprising, the government’s debt stood at Tk 18.32 lakh crore.

During the first 14 months of the interim government, the debt increased by approximately Tk 2.6 lakh crore. In the current government’s seven and a half months in office, net borrowing from banks has amounted to around Tk 79,000 crore.

Taken together, the government’s liabilities now stand at approximately Tk 23 lakh crore, a burden that ultimately falls on the people of the country. In the current budget, Tk 1,27,500 crore has been allocated solely for interest payments.

Against this backdrop, relations with development partners have become a major concern. Of the $5.5 billion programme with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Bangladesh has received $3.64 billion in five instalments. Last June, the IMF announced that Bangladesh had applied for a new programme.

Negotiating the terms and conditions is the sovereign right of any country, and that process is now underway. However, it is important to remember that budget support from the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank (ADB) depends to a considerable extent on the IMF’s assessment.

Another turning point lies ahead on this challenging path to economic growth: Bangladesh’s graduation from the least developed country (LDC) category, scheduled for 24 November 2026. At the government’s request, the United Nations Committee for Development Policy (CDP) has recommended extending the transition period until 2029. The final decision will come during the current session of the UN General Assembly.

In 2018, Bangladesh met the United Nations’ three criteria for the first time: gross national income per capita, the Human Assets Index, and the Economic and Environmental Vulnerability Index. After meeting the criteria for a second time in 2021, the Committee for Development Policy (CDP) recommended the country’s graduation.

However, in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, 2026 was set as the graduation year, with a five-year preparatory period instead of the usual three. Following graduation, Bangladesh will be classified as a developing country under the United Nations’ classification system.

In the current circumstances, securing additional time is reassuring, but time alone is not the solution. If this extended period is not used to pursue reforms and improve productivity and competitiveness, and if Bangladesh does not genuinely begin its journey beyond the lower-middle-income trap towards upper-middle-income status and a prosperous economy, the same crisis will return in an even more severe form three years from now.

The government has announced a target of building a $1 trillion economy by 2034. It is an ambitious vision, and the numbers are daunting. To double an economy worth $501 billion in eight years, Bangladesh would need to grow by an average of approximately 9 per cent annually in dollar terms, while real economic growth currently stands below 4 per cent.
The obstacles along the way are becoming increasingly apparent: stagnant investment, uncertainty over gas and electricity supplies for industries, a banking sector burdened by defaulted loans, a tax-to-GDP ratio of just 6.8 per cent, skills shortages, and uncertainty over the value of the taka and price stability. Announcing targets without removing these obstacles will only raise expectations and increase the pressure to deliver.

At the household level, preparation and financial literacy are also essential. These include keeping a simple record of income and expenditure, maintaining a small emergency fund, and avoiding high-interest loans.

Despite facing the same oil crisis, neighbouring India achieved 7.8 per cent economic growth in the first quarter of the current fiscal year, while keeping inflation at around 4.5 per cent. The success of Japan, South Korea, China and Singapore rests on similar foundations: price stability, policy consistency, a skilled workforce and a disciplined financial sector.
The question now is: where do we stand in comparison with these stable economies? A country plagued by various structural weaknesses will inevitably face crises, which may sometimes intensify. There is no denying this. The question is, what should be done to address them?

First, to control prices, action must be taken at the source of rising costs. A transparent, automatic fuel-pricing mechanism is needed to ensure that people fairly benefit when global prices fall, as well as when they rise. At the same time, unwarranted interference in markets and the transport sector must be firmly curbed.

Second, protecting the newly impoverished. The World Bank says that by accurately identifying eligible beneficiaries and coordinating family cards with cash assistance, an additional 2.85 million people could be lifted above the poverty line. An updated social registry is essential to achieve this.

Third, safeguarding industries and employment. Last May, Bangladesh Bank announced a Tk 600 billion stimulus package to revive closed factories, with the aim of creating 2.5 million jobs. The immediate priority is to ensure that this assistance is provided according to transparent criteria and on the condition that workers’ jobs are protected, while guaranteeing uninterrupted gas and electricity supplies to industries.

Fourth, reforming the banking and revenue sectors. The cycle of debt will not be broken without ending the practice of repeatedly rescheduling loans, seizing the assets of wilful defaulters, and raising the tax-to-GDP ratio to a standard level.

Fifth, ensuring policy clarity and consistency. A clear position on issues involving development partners, including the IMF, a medium-term debt strategy, and a roadmap for competitiveness in the post-LDC period could help restore investor confidence.

At the household level, preparation and financial literacy are also essential. These include keeping a simple record of income and expenditure, maintaining a small emergency fund, and avoiding high-interest loans. The countless young entrepreneurs across the country must receive the financial assistance and skills-development support they need to reach their full potential. They should also seek necessary guidance from financial institutions that work with young people.

Debates over who did what and who left behind how much debt may sometimes be politically important or serve as fodder for public argument. But far more urgent is getting the country’s future economic calculations right. The strain of this challenge is becoming increasingly visible every day in the shopping bags of working people, the pockets of salaried employees, and the shuttered factories of entrepreneurs.

There is only one task now: to bring every person in the country within the reach of development and move the nation forward through shared participation. In this topsy-turvy economic game, no single side can win alone; success requires everyone to win together.

There is nothing wrong with dreaming of a trillion-dollar economy. But in an economy where 2.1 million people fall into poverty in a single year and a vast population of young people faces the risk of unemployment, the first priority must be to secure firm footing, and summon the determination and enthusiasm needed to bounce back.

MM Mahbub Hasan is a banker, development researcher and writer.

item.title: Canada Express Entry: Up to 100 extra points for high-wage jobs, key changes announced
item.description:
CANADA-Express Entry-FLAG

The Canadian federal government has announced major changes to the Express Entry system, the popular pathway for applying for Permanent Residency (PR) in Canada.

Under the new policy, additional bonus points will be awarded in the Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) to candidates who hold high-wage job offers or are currently employed in high-paying occupations in Canada.

Senior immigration officials formally announced the new policy during a press conference on Friday (16 October). The decision was confirmed in an official government press release.

When the changes take effect, how points will be awarded

The new rules will come into effect on 3 November, 2026. Eligible candidates will automatically receive these bonus points in their Express Entry profiles.

New tiers of point distribution

According to official data, additional CRS points will be determined across three categories based on the National Median Wage of a specific occupation across Canada.

Points will be awarded after verifying the candidate’s job responsibilities under the National Occupational Classification (NOC):

  • Twice the median wage or higher: Earning at least double the median wage for the designated occupation will grant a maximum of 100 additional CRS points.

  • 1.5 Times the median wage or higher: Earning 1.5 times the median wage will yield 70 additional points.

  • 1.3 Times the median wage or higher: Earning 1.3 times the median wage will provide 50 additional points.

In addition, candidates whose prior Canadian work experience falls into high-wage categories will receive an extra bonus of 20 to 70 points, depending on their income level and duration of work.

LMIA requirement to be removed

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) confirmed that the requirement for a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) is being waived for high-wage job offers under this new policy.

This move is expected to make the application process simpler and significantly faster.

Why the policy change

The Canadian government’s primary goal is to accelerate economic growth by prioritizing skilled, merit-based professionals. Eligible candidates in high-wage sectors such as technical trades, healthcare, engineering, IT and senior corporate management will benefit the most from these updated CRS criteria.

Immigration experts believe that once the changes take effect on 3 November, CRS scores for high-earning professionals will jump much closer to the invitation cutoffs, paving the way for faster PR approval.

Candidates who do not fall into high-wage categories may face longer and more uncertain waiting periods in the applicant pool.

item.title: Cadet college admission circular published, applications open on 1 November, test marks reduced
item.description:
An admission circular has been published for enrolment in Class VII at the country's 12 cadet colleges for the 2027 academic year.

Applications will open at 8:00 am on 1 November 2026 and continue until 5:00 pm on 5 December 2026.

Students interested in taking the admission test must apply online. Applicants must submit their applications within the stipulated period through the websites www.cadetcollege.army.mil.bd or cadetcollegeadmission.army.bd.

Operated under the supervision of the Adjutant General's Branch of the Bangladesh Army, cadet colleges are residential educational institutions.

Alongside general education, these institutions provide extracurricular activities, leadership training and basic military training. The country has 12 cadet colleges, including nine for boys and three for girls.

Eligibility criteria

Students must have passed Class VI or an equivalent examination to apply for admission.

Both the applicant and their parents must be Bangladeshi citizens.

The applicant's age must not exceed 13 years and six months as of 1 January 2027.

The minimum height requirement is 4 feet 8 inches.

Applicants must also be physically and mentally fit.

When will the admission test be held?

The written admission test will be held on 26 December 2026, from 10:00 am to 1:00 pm.

How many marks will the admission test carry?

Admission to cadet colleges is generally completed in three stages: a written examination, a viva voce and a medical examination.

Among these, the written examination is the most important stage. Passing this examination means taking a significant step towards fulfilling the dream of getting into a cadet college.

Changes have been introduced to the cadet college admission test for 2027. The new syllabus was published earlier.

Under the revised syllabus, the total marks have been reduced by 100, bringing the written examination down from 300 to 200 marks.

After a long time, the cadet college admission test is returning to a 200-mark format.

According to the new syllabus, the examination will carry 65 marks in English, 70 in Mathematics and 45 in Bangla. Another 20 marks have been allocated for Science, Bangladesh and Global Studies, Information Technology, General Knowledge and Intelligence.

The examination will carry a total of 200 marks. Candidates can take the written examination in either Bangla or English.

The dates, times and venues for the viva voce and medical examinations of candidates who pass the written test will be published on the website later.

Candidates who pass all the examinations will be selected finally on the basis of merit.

How to apply

Interested students can apply by visiting the cadet college admission website and clicking on the ‘Apply Now’ option.

They must first register to obtain a user ID and password. After logging in, applicants must fill out the application form and upload the required documents and photographs.

How much is the application fee?

The application fee is Tk 2,500. It can be paid through bKash, Trust Bank's TAP, SSL Commerz, Nagad and Rocket.

Applicants are advised to read the instructions in the admission circular carefully before applying.

Detailed information and the full admission circular are available on the cadet college website.

item.title: Fire service: Cox’s Bazar resort lacked fire safety licence
item.description:
Tup Tup Restaurant and Resort, located in the Patuartek beach area along Marine Drive in Inani, Ukhia, Cox’s Bazar, did not have a fire safety licence, Fire Service and Civil Defence Director General Brigadier General Sultanul Afrin Junaid said on Saturday afternoon.
The death toll from the fire at the resort has risen to 10. Preliminary information indicates that all the victims were tourists visiting the area.
The six victims initially identified were Israt Jahan Maliha, 30, and Milita Mehejabin Alvi, 23, from Banasree, Dhaka; Laila Jahan Nabila, 27, and Nafista Mim, 27, from Khilgaon, Dhaka; and Fariha Kabir, 33, and Fayizan Ahmed, 5, from Chuadanga.
Those injured in the incident were initially taken to Ukhia Upazila Health Complex before being transferred to Cox’s Bazar District Sadar Hospital, according to the hospital’s emergency department.
Around 30 people were reportedly at the resort when the fire broke out. Four to five people managed to escape, but the whereabouts and condition of the others remain unconfirmed.
According to the Fire Service, it received a report of the fire at 7:25am. The resort is about 18km from the fire station, and firefighters arrived at the scene at 8am.
Two units from Ukhia Fire Station brought the blaze under control by 8:15am. Six bodies were initially recovered from the site, while four other victims later died.

item.title: How fire started at Tup-Tup Resort in Cox’s Bazar
item.description:
An electrical short circuit triggered a fire at Tup-Tup Resort along Marine Drive in Cox’s Bazar on Saturday morning, according to the resort’s person in charge, Suman.
The blaze reportedly intensified after an air conditioner and a gas cylinder exploded, spreading fire throughout the building and leaving at least 10 people dead.
Earlier, the Fire Service reported six deaths, saying preliminary information suggested that all the victims were tourists. Senior Fire Service official Dolan Acharya confirmed the information.
The six victims initially identified were Israt Jahan Maliha, 30, and Milita Mehejabin Alvi, 23, from Banasree, Dhaka; Laila Jahan Nabila, 27, and Nafista Mim, 27, from Khilgaon, Dhaka; and Fariha Kabir, 33, and Fayizan Ahmed, 5, from Chuadanga.
Those injured in the fire were initially taken to Ukhiya Upazila Health Complex before being transferred to Cox’s Bazar District Sadar Hospital, according to the hospital’s emergency department.
Two Fire Service units responded to the incident. Local residents said the fire broke out at around 7:30am. Firefighters arrived shortly afterwards, while residents and police joined rescue efforts and attempts to bring the blaze under control.
Around 30 people were reportedly at the resort when the fire started. Four to five people managed to escape, but the whereabouts and condition of the others remain unconfirmed.

item.title: PM visits 13 locations across Dhaka to inspect public services
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Saturday made surprise visits to 13 locations across Dhaka, including hospitals, educational institutions and government residential quarters to assess the quality of public services, cleanliness and overall management.
Starting at 9:10am, the prime minister visited different areas of Dhaka until 1:41pm, speaking to officials and examining cleanliness, service quality and overall management at various facilities, said his Deputy Press Secretary Hasan Shiplu.
He first visited Kuwait-Bangladesh Friendship Government Hospital in Uttara, followed by Rajuk Uttara Model College and Mirpur Cantonment Public School and College.
He then visited the National Heart Foundation of Bangladesh at Mirpur, Paikpara Staff Quarters and Government Bangla College.
The prime minister later inspected Bangladesh Shishu Hospital and Institute and Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College and Hospital at Agargaon.
He also visited his old college Dhaka Residential Model College, where he addressed students and urged them to help build a clean Bangladesh and plant more trees.
Tarique subsequently visited Dhanmondi Government Boys' High School, Kalabagan Staff Quarters and Azimpur Government Officers' and Employees' Residential Quarters.
Expressing dissatisfaction with poor cleanliness and management at several locations, the prime minister gave the authorities concerned two weeks to improve cleanliness at the Azimpur government quarters.
Earlier, during his visit to Kuwait-Bangladesh Friendship Government Hospital, he gave the authorities seven days to improve the hospital's environment and cleanliness arrangements.
During his visit to Bangladesh Shishu Hospital and Institute, Tarique found Associate Professor Dr Rafiqul Islam smoking in his untidy room.
He immediately instructed the hospital chairman to take action against the doctor, who was subsequently suspended him.
The prime minister also visited a footpath freed from hawkers at Mirpur-10.
Dhaka North City Corporation Administrator Shafiqul Islam Khan Milton was present during the visit.
Throughout the surprise inspections, Tarique spoke to officials, students and members of the public, stressing the need for responsible action by the authorities concerned to improve public services, maintain cleanliness and protect public health.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,189 as three die in 24 hours
item.description:
Three more children have died from measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours leading up to 8:00am on Saturday, raising the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak to 1,189.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all three of the latest casualties as suspected.
With the latest figures, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,085, while the number of confirmed deaths remained unchanged at 104, as no new confirmed measles deaths were reported in the last 24 hours.
Among the three new suspected fatalities, the highest concentration was recorded in Chittagong, with two deaths reported in both the Chittagong division and Chittagong district.
A total of 950 suspected measles cases were recorded in the 24 hours till Saturday morning, taking the overall suspected case tally to 211,990.
During the same period, 85 new confirmed measles cases were reported, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 23,057.
Since March 15, 2026, a total of 188,452 suspected measles patients have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 180,848 have recovered and been discharged from hospitals, according to the DGHS.

item.title: Legal notice seeks probe into possible use of dengue as biological weapon
item.description:
A legal notice has been served on the government seeking a high-level scientific investigation into the unusually high dengue mortality in Bangladesh and possible genetic mutations of the virus, including an inquiry into allegations that it could be linked to a covert biological attack.
The notice also demands the establishment of an internationally accredited research laboratory to prevent and investigate biological weapons threats.
Supreme Court lawyer Md Mahmudul Hasan Mamun served the notice on Saturday in the public interest.
It was addressed to the secretaries of the ministries of defence, home affairs, health and family welfare, and foreign affairs, as well as the administrators of Dhaka North and South city corporations. A copy was also sent to the United Nations resident coordinator in Bangladesh.
The notice describes dengue as a severe public health crisis rather than a routine illness, arguing that the recurring deaths and growing number of cases warrant investigation beyond conventional mosquito-control measures.
Citing books on biological warfare and medical research, Mamun, who is also studying for a Master of Public Health degree, refers to historical accounts of plans to use disease-carrying insects in biological attacks.
The notice cites The A to Z of Nuclear, Biological, and Chemical Warfare (2019), by Benjamin C Garrett and John Hart, which discusses a Japanese military plan during World War II, codenamed “Operation PX”. According to the notice, the plan involved releasing insects carrying pathogens linked to dengue, plague, cholera and typhus along the US coast.
It also refers to Anthony Tu’s book Chemical and Biological Weapons and Terrorism (2018), which the notice says discusses the classification of dengue virus among biological agents considered for weaponisation by the US military.
Another reference is Advances in Biological and Chemical Terrorism Countermeasures (2008), edited by Ronald J Kendall and other experts. The notice cites the publication in support of its concerns about the potential misuse of disease-causing agents.
The notice argues that Bangladesh’s high population density and mosquito prevalence, alongside the reported severity of recent dengue outbreaks, warrant an urgent scientific and forensic investigation. It calls for epidemiologists, virologists and public health specialists to examine the virus’s genetic characteristics, origin and transmission mechanisms to determine whether there is evidence of deliberate or artificial modification.
However, the notice does not present evidence establishing that the dengue outbreak in Bangladesh resulted from a biological attack.
Mamun also cites Bangladesh’s obligations under international law, noting that the country is a signatory to the Biological Weapons Convention (BWC). He refers to Articles I and X of the convention, which prohibit biological weapons and address the peaceful use of biological science, as well as United Nations Security Council Resolution 1540 of 2004, which requires states to take measures against the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction.
The notice further invokes Articles 18(1) and 32 of the Constitution of Bangladesh, concerning the state’s responsibility to improve public health and the right to life.
It asks the authorities to arrange an expert-led genetic and forensic investigation into the dengue virus within 10 days to assess whether there is any evidence of an artificial biological attack. It also calls for the immediate establishment of a high-security laboratory for research into biological weapons prevention and comprehensive, science-based measures to control Aedes mosquitoes.
The notice warns that failure to meet the demands could lead to a public interest litigation petition before the High Court Division of the Supreme Court under Article 102 of the Constitution, seeking measures to protect public health, national security and citizens’ lives.

item.title: 5 killed in Kurigram road crash
item.description:
At least five people, including a mother and her two children, were killed in a collision between a truck and a battery-powered auto-rickshaw in Rowmari upazila of Kurigram on Saturday.
The accident occurred near Shiberdangi Bazar in Jadurchar Union around noon. Four of the deceased were members of the same family, according to preliminary information.
Roumari Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Kawsar Ali confirmed the deaths.
“I am at the scene. The bodies of three people, including two women and a man, have been sent to the hospital. I have learned that two children who were taken to the hospital in critical condition have also died. We are collecting further details,” he said.
According to Roumari Health Complex authorities, the children were identified as Rishad and Tuba. Their mother Lipi and maternal aunt Sharifa were also killed. They were residents of Chatalakanda village in the upazila.
Upazila Health and Family Planning Officer (UHFPO) Dr Abdus Samad said five bodies had been recovered so far, including those of two children and two women.
“The two children, their mother and maternal aunt are among the deceased. The identity of the male victim has not yet been confirmed, but he is believed to be the auto-rickshaw driver,” he said.

item.title: Humaiun leads Bangladesh delegation to Baghdad OIC meeting
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir is leading the Bangladesh delegation to the 52nd session of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers, which is underway in the Iraqi capital Baghdad.
The council is being held under the theme “Dialogue and solidarity, two fundamental pillars for promoting peace and sustainable development”.
The state minister is expected to deliver Bangladesh’s country statement on Saturday and hold a number of bilateral meetings with his counterparts from OIC member states on the sidelines of the session, said a Foreign Ministry press release on Saturday.
On Sunday, he will also co-chair an ad hoc ministerial meeting on accountability for human rights violations against the Rohingyas.
Host Iraq has taken over the chairmanship of the Council of Foreign Ministers from Türkiye for a one-year term.

item.title: Fakir Lalon Shah’s 136th death anniversary program begins in Kushtia
item.description:
A three-day program marking the 136th death anniversary of Baul mystic Fakir Lalon Shah began at his shrine in Chheuriya Akhra Bari in Kumarkhali upazila of the district on Saturday, drawing thousands of devotees, followers and visitors from home and abroad.
The program, which will continue until Monday, October 19, is being organized by the Kushtia district administration under the supervision of Lalon Academy, with support from the Ministry of Cultural Affairs.
Cultural Affairs Minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury, MP, is scheduled to inaugurate the formal program at the Lalon Academy premises this evening. Cultural Affairs Adviser Dr Zahed Ur Rahman will attend as the guest of honor.
Deputy Commissioner and Lalon Academy President Md Touhid Bin-Hasan will chair the inaugural ceremony. Noted essayist Dr Rashidun Nabi will deliver the keynote address.
Former Kushtia district BNP president and former lawmaker Syed Mehedi Ahmed Rumi, Kushtia-1 lawmaker Reza Ahammed, reserved-seat MP Mst Farida Yeasmin, Additional Secretary of the Ministry of Cultural Affairs AKM Abdullah Khan and Kushtia Superintendent of Police Aminul Islam will attend as special guests.
Lalon devotees and spiritual practitioners Hridoy Shah and Asma Khanam will deliver welcome addresses on behalf of Lalon Academy.
Following the inaugural ceremony and discussion, renowned Baul singers from across the country and performers of Lalon Academy will present Lalon songs on the Lalon stage at night.
Beyond the formal program, the shrine has become a gathering place for devotees who come to commemorate the mystic through spiritual practices, songs and discussions reflecting his philosophy of humanity, equality and self-discovery.
Many devotees arrived at the Akhra Bari a day or two ahead of the anniversary. They are participating in traditional morning and afternoon devotional services and holding small gatherings where they exchange Lalon’s teachings through songs.
At the shrine’s auditorium, Baul followers were seen performing with traditional instruments, including the dotara, while hundreds of curious listeners gathered to enjoy their soulful renditions.
Fakir Rashid Shah, a devotee who has taken shelter in a corner of the shrine complex, said the spiritual significance of the occasion should not be overshadowed by formal celebrations.
He added that devotees travel long distances to find spiritual peace and fulfil their inner longing through Lalon’s teachings.
Baul practitioner Hridoy Shah said the annual gathering was an important part of the lives of those who follow Lalon’s philosophy.
Drawing a parallel with the Greek philosopher Socrates’ famous dictum, “Know thyself,” he said Lalon’s teachings continued to inspire humanity and self-awareness in everyday life.
Lalon Shah died on October 17, 1890, corresponding to the first day of Kartik in the Bengali year 1297. His death anniversary has been observed at Chheuriya for generations, with devotees considering the shrine a sacred destination for spiritual reflection and communion.
This year’s observance seeks to uphold the mystic’s enduring message of humanity and universal brotherhood through discussions, devotional practices and cultural performances.
Lalon Academy President and Kushtia Deputy Commissioner Md Touhid Bin-Hasan said all preparations for the three-day program had been completed.
“Like previous years, we have taken all necessary administrative measures to ensure the discussions on Lalon’s philosophy and songs, along with the cultural programs, are held safely and peacefully,” he said.

item.title: Bangladesh return to ODIs, face Zimbabwe in tri-series opener
item.description:
Bangladesh begin their UAE ODI Tri-Series 2026 campaign against Zimbabwe at the Zayed Cricket Stadium in Abu Dhabi on Saturday.
The match starts at 5:30pm Bangladesh time, with T Sports and Nagorik TV set to telecast it live.
The Tigers return to ODI action after three months, having played a T20 series against Zimbabwe in July before touring Australia for a Test series in August.
The three-team tournament also features Afghanistan, against whom Bangladesh played a one-off Test at the same venue earlier this week, with the match ending in a draw.
Bangladesh's last ODI was also against Zimbabwe, with the Tigers securing a seven-wicket victory after the hosts had already sealed the three-match series.
The two sides will meet at a neutral venue for the first time in 20 years.
While this will be Zimbabwe's first ODI at the Zayed Cricket Stadium, Bangladesh have played six matches at the venue, winning two.
The series will test the ODI credentials of the three teams, who are ranked between eighth and 11th in the latest ICC Men's ODI Team Rankings.
Bangladesh are targeting the title, with batter Mosaddek Hossain stressing the importance of winning both round-robin matches against their opponents.
"We want to win the trophy, definitely, but to do that, we have to win both the (round-robin) matches against Zimbabwe and Afghanistan."
Mosaddek also expressed hope that the players would adapt well to the conditions in Abu Dhabi.
"Our Test players adjusted to the heat pretty well. We have trained for a few days here so we hope there will be a bit of breeze in the evening, since the matches will start in the late afternoon," he said.
Zimbabwe and Afghanistan will face off in the second match on Monday, before Bangladesh take on Afghanistan on Wednesday. The final is scheduled for Friday.

item.title: Haze triggers highest-level alert in parts of Southeast Asia
item.description:
Fires in Indonesia that have sent toxic smoke and disrupted daily life across Southeast Asia have triggered the highest-level alert by the regional bloc’s meteorological monitor.
The months-long pollution spell has closed schools, fueled a surge in respiratory conditions and restricted outdoor activities in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and East Timor.
“This thing needs to stop,” Zul Hafiz, a 39-year-old teacher cycling from the Malaysian city of Shah Alam to the capital, told AFP on Saturday, calling on the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) to take action.
The 11-country organization’s Asean Specialized Meteorological Centre (ASMC) said in a notice on its website on Friday that it had activated “Alert Level 3 for the Southern Asean region” -- the highest rung of a four-tiered alert system.
The alert level is triggered when there is a “high risk of severe transboundary haze in the region” and is reserved for widespread moderate to dense smoke haze, observed over two or more consecutive days.
The ASMC has already issued two Level 3 alerts this year, according to its website.
Singapore ranked second on IQAir’s live ranking of the world’s most polluted major cities behind Baghdad on Saturday, with Kuala Lumpur third. All readings showed “very hazardous” levels.”
Indonesia said Saturday it had been using dry ice at one of South Sumatra province’s main airports in an attempt to disperse the haze.
The country’s national disaster mitigation agency said that 2.4 tons of dry ice were dispersed by plane.
“The smoke not only reduces visibility and disrupts aircraft operations, but also affects residents’ health,” the agency warned.
The haze has disrupted life across Southeast Asia, sparking fresh calls for action from those affected.
“It’s a bit unfair on Malaysia because of the irresponsible behavior of our neighboring country,” Khairul Azhar, a 33-year-old bank officer told AFP in Kuala Lumpur.
“This is affecting our weekend routine -- not just for us but many Malaysians,” he said.
In Indonesia’s Palangkaraya -- part of the epicenter of the fires where thick haze turned the skies into apocalyptic shades of yellow and orange -- residents said they were suffering from its effects on Saturday.
“The haze has a big impact on us, especially on health and the economy, with our income decreasing,” said Marzuki, a 38-year-old mechanic who like many in Indonesia, goes by only one name.
“Right now the economy is already very difficult, and the haze just makes it worse,” he told AFP, adding that this year’s situation was worse than even previous major bouts of haze in 2015.
“Hopefully it rains soon, the fires go out, and the smoke disappears so that activities can return to normal and it’s easier to earn a living again,” he said.
Joko, 51, a construction worker, said he had no choice but to keep on working or he would lose out on income.
“The thick smoke, when inhaled, makes it hard to breathe and stings the eyes, but what else can you do? This is how we earn a living,” Joko said, explaining he had no fixed income and relied on daily wage jobs.
In East Timor, unhealthy air pollution persisted on Saturday, including in the capital Dili, according to IQAir.
Authorities warned that the situation may worsen on Saturday and schools were closed.
Singapore said Friday it would issue warnings to seven companies in Indonesia it identified as responsible for the fires.
Philippines foreign department spokesman for Asean issues, Dominic Xavier Imperial, said Friday that the haze would be discussed at upcoming meetings ahead of a November Asean summit in Manila.

item.title: Russia hails Trump waiving sanctions as ‘historic’
item.description:
Russia on Saturday hailed US President Donald Trump’s move to waive new sanctions on it as “historic,” as Ukraine worries he is taking Moscow’s side in Europe’s worst conflict since World War II.
Trump signed an executive order Friday that waived sweeping US sanctions targeting Russia’s energy revenues amid a clash with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
The decision came despite Russia increasing strikes on Ukraine -- especially its capital, Kyiv -- in the fifth year of its offensive, which has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
“The Trump administration’s suspension of the Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment,” Kirill Dmitriev, envoy for Russian President Vladimir Putin, said on social media.
The Lindsey Graham Act -- named after the deceased US senator who sponsored the bill -- targeted Russia’s energy and defense sectors, as well as Putin and the so-called “shadow fleet” of tankers used by Moscow to circumvent Western sanctions.
The Kremlin and Putin have not yet reacted to the move, which is a major diplomatic win for Moscow.
Dmitriev said the act would have caused “serious damage first and foremost to the US economy and global markets.”
Trump’s waiver comes after he struck a deal with Putin to ease existing sanctions on Russia in exchange for Moscow releasing large amounts of diesel onto global markets.
He announced the executive order Friday, shortly after Putin appeared in military uniform and said Moscow aims to capture the rest of east Ukraine.
US-led talks to end the war in Ukraine have not led to a breakthrough. Both Putin and Zelensky have frustrated Trump in the past with a lack of progress in halting the grinding war.
The move is bound to spook Ukraine’s European allies, who worry the White House is taking the Kremlin’s side.
Zelensky rallied his allies Friday on a visit to Brussels for a European Union summit, urging them to keep financing Ukraine’s fight and insisting he was standing up for his country amid the row with Trump.
Russian forces struck Ukraine’s southern city of Kherson Saturday after Trump’s announcement, killing one person and wounding 22, local officials said.
Russia has increased strikes on Kyiv in recent weeks, squeezing the city as Ukrainians brace for another winter of war.
Ukraine has been struggling to shoot down Russian missiles and has been left scrambling to boost defenses ahead of winter.
Russia controls large swathes of eastern and southern Ukraine and Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine by force.
“On the whole I see a positive trend in the operations of the troop groupings,” Putin told army leaders Friday, dressed in military attire.
“Undoubtedly, one of the main objectives remains the liberation of the Donetsk People’s Republic,” he added, using the Kremlin’s name for the eastern Donetsk region.
European leaders put on a show of unity with Zelensky Friday as he grappled with Trump.
“This is no time to withdraw support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia’s sanctions,” said European Council chief Antonio Costa.
“Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure.”
European concerns have been heightened by disruptions to a critical US-provided satellite system that has hampered Ukraine’s ability to counter Russia’s intense bombardments.

item.title: PM makes surprise visits to 13 sites, urges cleanliness
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman today paid surprise visits to 13 establishments including schools, hospitals, residential areas and public spaces in the capital to assess the cleanliness and overall managements of the institutions.

During his four and half hours long visits beginning from 9:10am, he went to Kuwait Bangladesh Friendship Government Hospital in Uttara, Rajuk Uttara Model College, Mirpur Cantonment Public School and College, National Heart Foundation, Paikpara Staff Quarters, Government Bangla College, Bangladesh Shishu Hospital and Institute and Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College and Hospital in Agargaon.

The Prime Minister also visited his former educational institution Dhaka Residential Model College in the city’s Mohammadpur area.

Apart from these, he visited Dhanmondi Government Boys' High School, Kalabagan Staff Quarters and Azimpur Government Officers and Employees' Residential Quarters and the footpaths in Mirpur-10 that had been cleared of hawker encroachment.

During the visits, he talked to officials, students, patients, residents and pedestrians and people to assess the conditions at different establishments.

While visiting Kuwait Bangladesh Friendship Government Hospital, the Prime Minister expressed dissatisfaction with the hospital's cleanliness and overall management and gave the authorities seven days to improve the situation.

He spoke to patients about their treatment and inspected different departments, including the intensive care unit (ICU) and operation theatres.

At Bangladesh Shishu Hospital and Institute, the Prime Minister found Associate Professor Rafiqul Islam smoking in his unhygienic room and instructed the hospital chairman to take action against him. The physician was later temporarily suspended.

At Azimpur government residential quarters, the Prime Minister expressed strong displeasure over the unhygienic environment and gave the authorities two weeks to ensure visible improvements in cleanliness and make the residential area habitable.

Residents also raised complaints about the area's unhygienic conditions and law and order situation. The Prime Minister listened to their concerns and asked the authorities concerned to take necessary measures to address the issues.

During his visit to the footpaths in Mirpur-10, Tarique Rahman asked pedestrians whether the removal of hawkers had made their movement easier and whether they were still facing difficulties.


He stressed the need to keep footpaths free from encroachment and ensure unobstructed movement for pedestrians.

The Prime Minister addressed students and members of the Bangladesh National Cadet Corps (BNCC) and Scouts at Government Bangla College and urged them to take an active role in building a clean and healthy Bangladesh and planting more trees.

He emphasised that keeping homes, educational institutions and surrounding areas clean was essential to preventing dengue and protecting public health, calling for collective efforts to ensure a clean and liveable environment for future generations.

Throughout the visits, the Prime Minister stressed the need for responsible performance of duties by officials and effective measures to improve public services, cleanliness, healthcare and the overall management of public institutions.

State Minister for LGRD and Cooperatives Mir Shahe Alam, Dhaka North City Corporation Administrator Shafiqul Islam Khan Milton and Dhaka South City Corporation Administrator Abdus Salam accompanied the Prime Minister during his visits.

item.title: Cox's Bazar resort fire: Nur Alam loses wife, son, 4 other relatives
item.description:
“My wife had been ill for some time. Even so, she went to Cox’s Bazar to spend time with family members. I had gone with them too. After reaching Cox’s Bazar, I returned to Chuadanga on Friday because of official work. When I learnt about the fire from the media on Saturday morning, I hurriedly made enquiries and discovered that six of those who had died were members of my family.”

Nur Alam, a senior marketing officer at the pharmaceutical company Drug International, who is based in Chuadanga, said this while speaking to Prothom Alo over the phone.

Ten people were killed when a fire broke out at a wooden resort on Patuartek Beach in Inani, Ukhiya, Cox’s Bazar, around 7:30 am on Saturday.

Cox’s Bazar resort fire: 6 family members die, man survives by jumping from first floor

Six of the victims belonged to the same family. They were Nur Alam’s wife, Faria Kabir, 33; their five-year-old son, Faizan Nur; his brother-in-law, Nasir Uddin, 25; and his three sisters-in-law, Israt Jahan Maliha, 30, Laila Jahan Nabila, 27, and Milita Mehezabin Alvi, 23. Another victim was Nafista Mim, 27.

Apart from Nur Alam’s family members, the other victims lived in the capital’s Banasree and Khilgaon areas. The identities of the remaining three people killed have yet to be established.

Six people injured in the fire are receiving treatment at Cox’s Bazar Sadar Hospital. They are Mugda Medical College Hospital physician Shihab Uddin, 31; his wife, Nafiza Newaz Khan, 29; Ismail Hossain Masud, 30, and his wife, Meherun Nessa, 27; Mannan, 34; and Samida, 32.

Fire breaks out at Cox’s Bazar resort, six bodies recovered, six injured, all victims tourists

The injured Ismail Hossain and his wife, Meherun Nessa, are Faria Kabir’s maternal uncle and aunt. Their home is in South Thetalia village in Matlab North upazila, Chandpur. This information was provided by a relative of the victims Mohammad Ahad, a student at Jagannath University.

Nur Alam’s home is in Gazirpar village in Barakotha Union of Uzirpur upazila, Barishal. He has been working in Chuadanga for about eight years. Because of his job, he and his family lived in a rented house in the Dakshin Hospitalpara area of Chuadanga town.

Nur Alam said he had travelled to Cox’s Bazar last Thursday with his wife, Faria Kabir, their son, Faizan Nur, and members of his in-laws’ family, including his brother-and sisters-in-law. Before that, he had travelled from Chuadanga to Dhaka with his wife and son on Wednesday.

Fire breaks out at Cox’s Bazar resort, 10 dead, 6 victims identified

Local residents said the fire broke out at Tuptup Resort, beside Marine Drive, at around 7:30 am. Fire service personnel arrived after being alerted. Local residents later began efforts to control the fire and rescue those trapped, with police assistance.

At around 2:15 pm, Cox’s Bazar Fire Service Assistant Director Syed Morshed Hossain confirmed to Prothom Alo that 10 bodies had been recovered. He said there could be more bodies and that the rescue operation was continuing.

Ahad, a relative of the victims, said they had been scheduled to leave for Dhaka on Saturday morning. Everyone was overwhelmed with grief following the incident. It was difficult to come to terms with the deaths of so many relatives at once, he said.

item.title: 10 tourists killed in fire at Inani resort flagged as risky in June: Fire Service
item.description:
The Tuptup Resort, damaged in a fire at Inani in Ukhiya, Cox’s Bazar, had been operating without any approval from the Fire Service, said Fire Service and Civil Defence Director General Brigadier General Sultanul Afreen Junaid.

He said the resort had been identified as “risky” following an inspection in June and served with a notice. However, it continued operating illegally, disregarding the warning.

The director general disclosed the information at a press conference held in the conference room of the Fire Service and Civil Defence headquarters on Kazi Alauddin Road in Dhaka on Saturday afternoon. The press conference was primarily organised to outline the department’s fire safety preparations for Durga Puja.

A fire broke out at the wooden resort near Patowartek beach in Inani, Ukhiya upazila of Cox’s Bazar, around 7:30am on Saturday. Firefighters brought the blaze under control around 11:30am. By 1:30pm, the Fire Service had confirmed the recovery of 10 bodies from the resort. Six people who suffered burns were receiving treatment at Cox’s Bazar Sadar Hospital.

Fire breaks out at Cox’s Bazar resort, 10 dead, 6 victims identified

Fire Service Director General Sultanul Afreen Junaid said the three-storey wooden resort had a restaurant on the ground floor, where food was prepared, while the second and third floors accommodated tourists. However, the establishment did not have a fire safety certificate as required under Fire Service regulations and oversight.

Sultanul Afreen said the Fire Service received information about the fire around 7:30am. The nearest fire station was about 22 kilometres from the scene. Firefighters reached the site promptly after receiving the report, brought the blaze under control and subsequently extinguished it completely.

Asked about the safety and legality of resorts made of wood and other flammable materials at tourist destinations across the country, including Cox’s Bazar, the director general said many had not obtained the necessary permits. The authorities would contact the operators and take steps to bring them under the notice process, he said. Safety messages would also be communicated through the Cox’s Bazar Development Authority and relevant associations.

Warning that the risk of such incidents could increase during the upcoming dry season, the director general said those concerned needed to remain alert.

Regarding the cause of the fire, he said it would be possible to determine the origin after a thorough investigation. He also said the Fire Service would review existing laws, limitations in monitoring and possible courses of action to address cases in which risky establishments continue operating despite receiving notices, and to ensure effective measures against similar resorts nationwide.

Special vehicles planned to reach narrow roads quickly

Speaking about frequent fires, unauthorised factories and warehouses, and the risks posed by explosive materials in Old Dhaka, the director general said narrow roads in densely populated areas and the lack of adequate space between buildings posed major challenges for the Fire Service.

These conditions make it difficult for firefighters to reach incident sites quickly with heavy firefighting vehicles and equipment, he said.

He stressed the importance of complying with building codes and relevant regulations during construction. Ensuring all safety measures in old residential areas overnight would be difficult and time-consuming, he said.

Despite repeated efforts to raise awareness about compliance with regulations for new buildings, many people continued to disregard them.

Outlining alternative plans to overcome these limitations and improve response capacity, the director general said the department was planning to use specialised three-wheeled vehicles to reach congested areas and narrow roads quickly.

The department was also considering whether firefighters could carry hoses on motorcycles, connect them to water reservoirs in nearby buildings and use the water to extinguish fires immediately, he added.

item.title: "My 3 sisters lost 5 children, they came to visit in a group of 9"
item.description:
"Six of my nephews and nieces have died. I have three sisters. I am the only brother. Five of my three sisters' children died. The eldest niece's child also died. They had come for a vacation in a group of nine. Three survived," Aminul Islam lamented.

He is a resident of the capital city Dhaka.

On Saturday morning, around 7: 30AM, a fire at the wooden Tuptup Resort on the Patuartek beach of Inani in Ukhiya, Cox's Bazar, claimed the lives of six of his family members. On hearing the news, he flew from Dhaka to Cox's Bazar.

At around 2 PM today, Aminul Islam shared this information with journalists at Cox's Bazar Sadar Hospital.

He said, "They were supposed to return to Dhaka around 10:30 AM today. They came to Cox’s Bazar for a vacation last Thursday. When the fire broke out in the morning, two of them were outside. They informed me of the incident."

The resort where the fire broke out at Inani in Ukhiya, Cox’s Bazar, is named Tuptup. At 2:15PM today, Cox’s Bazar Fire Service Deputy Assistant Director Syed Morshed Hossain confirmed to Prothom Alo that ten bodies were recovered in the incident.

He mentioned that there could be more bodies. The rescue operation is ongoing.

According to local sources, the fire started at the resort adjacent to Marine Drive road at around 7: 30 AM. On receiving the news, the fire service personnel reached the scene. Later, local residents, with police assistance, began controlling and rescue operations.

Fire Service and Civil Defence Chattogram Division’s Deputy Director Md Toufikul Islam Bhuiyan said that Cox’s Bazar Fire Service was notified of the fire at 7: 23 AM today.

The fire service team arrived at the site around 8 AM. The fire was brought under control at 8: 15 AM. Four people died in the two toilets on the third floor.

Toufikul Islam Bhuiyan stated that strong winds from the sea quickly spread the fire in the wooden resort.

Such establishments need to have portable fire extinguishers, fire alarms, hoses, and fire safety plans. But none of these were present in the resort. There was no fire licence either. The resort had been built only seven or eight months ago.

He also mentioned that there was a dispute over the ownership of the place.

Among the deceased, identities of six have been confirmed—Dhaka's Ishrat Jahan Maliha (30), Milita Mehezabin Alvi (23), Laila Jahan Nabila (27), Nafishta Mim (27), Chuadanga’s Fariha Kabir (33), and five-year-old Faizan Ahmed.

Among the six identified, five are women and one is a child.

Six burn victims from the incident are being treated at Cox's Bazar Sadar Hospital.

Among them are Mugda Medical College Hospital’s doctor Shihab Uddin (31) and his wife Nafiza Nawaz Khan (29).

item.title: Being ‘arrogant’ without actually being arrogant
item.description:
There comes a point in almost everyone’s life when he or she discovers an uncomfortable truth: Being nice to everyone is not necessarily a sign of good character. Sometimes it is unnecessary courtesy and benevolence shown to the wrong people. And sometimes the recipient considers your politeness as sheer weakness.

However, this reality is seemingly pre-dominant in most of our workplaces particularly, in a newspaper office. Given my significant experience in the English print media journalism, I found that most of the time I had been and still am surrounded by three types of people : Those who produce the newspaper, those who discuss how the newspaper should be produced, and those who somehow manage to do neither while unrelentingly voicing strong opinions about everyone else's performance.

Let us assume our character to be Mr F.

Mr F is the editorial chief of a respected English-language newspaper. He is professional, experienced and, disturbing for his enemies since he is good at his job. He could take a chaotic pile of news reports, political statements, and press releases badly and wildly translated copies and turn them into a coherent article before the one and only serving of muri-chanachur reaches his table. Penning an editorial is usually a piece of cake for him. He also mingles freely with everyone. This, as he eventually discovers, is his first mistake.

He believes in the old-fashioned Bengali virtues: Respect your elders, listen to people, don't unnecessarily hurt anyone's feelings, offer tea, help the junior colleague, answer the message, and return the phone call. In other words, Mr F behaves as if civilisation in this part of the world is still functioning.

However, his colleagues are often equipped with other ideas.
There is Mr X, whose key professional achievement has been to survive in the same position for 35 years. There is Ms Y, who had perfected the technique of looking extremely busy while producing remarkably little. And there is Mr Z, who had never written a memorable headline in his life but somehow had developed a PhD-level expertise in explaining why everybody else's headline is always wrong.

They may not be incompetent in the dramatic sense. But they are something even more interesting: Comfortably Mediocre. They had climbed-up that beautiful professional hilltop (Please read the newspaper office) where ambition had died long ago, but resentment remained surprisingly fit.

Mr F's success therefore presented them with a daily existential threat. He isn't rude to them. No point competing with them. He isn't even particularly interested in them. This is surely intolerable, since nothing annoys a mediocre person quite like discovering that the person they dislike continuously ignores them.

So the small manipulative moves began to turn Mr F reactive. A crude remark said every now and then. Insults are hurled through a third party, so that it reaches Mr F through another colleague and then via another one. Mr F uses designer brand perfume kept free for all on top of his desk, but his foes compare the fragrance often with a corpse surrounded by incensed sticks. Or a meeting where Mr F's advice was carefully and collectively ignored and then, five minutes later repeated and endorsed by the editor to great applause.

At times it seems like a silent whisper in the corridor or a raised eyebrow. A typical “Ami kichhu bolini, but…” followed by an entire indictment of the man's character. And then comes the classic workplace accusation: F has become arrogant.

This surely puzzles Mr F. He has not become arrogant. He has simply become tired. Here comes the crucial distinction between becoming arrogant without knowledge and authority and becoming arrogant in an artful way.

Blind arrogance says, “I am superior to you.” Artful arrogance says, “I have more important things to do.”

Unfortunately, to people accustomed to having access to your attention, the second can look exactly like the first. This is where many good people get into trouble. They think if they stop explaining themselves, people will misunderstand them.

They are correct. People will misunderstand them anyway. Mr F slowly discovers that some people do not interpret generosity as generosity. They interpret it as availability. Some do not interpret politeness as kindness. They interpret it as a flaw as well.

And some do not interpret silence as dignity. They interpret it as an invitation to continue talking about you. You are most welcome to either agree or disagree; this is where a little constructive arrogance becomes useful.

It is not the “Do you know who I am?” type. That sort of arrogance is usually found in people whose CV requires several pages to explain who they are.
However, Mr F''s carefully crafted stoic arrogance says just a “Thank you”, and then doing absolutely nothing.

Someone offers unsolicited advice? “Thank you”. Someone tries to provoke him? His reply is “Interesting”. Someone delivers office gossip? “Oh I see.” Someone attempts to explain why a mediocre decision was actually brilliant? “Fair enough” And now it is time to leave office.

Purely a personal remark - a Dhaka workplace, like the British Empire, was never designed to survive such passive resistance. People wanted emotional reactions. Mr F, however, only gives them punctuation these days. They expected arguments. He offers them either deluxe or single malt, and they refuse it considering it poisonous. They expect arguments, explanations and hyper reactive outbursts.

As he gives his opponents silence, soon the office corridor begins to buzz. “Mr F has isolated himself, what is the strategy behind it.” “He doesn't talk to people anymore.” “He has become very distant.”

This last accusation is particularly amusing since Mr F had spent years mixing with one and all. He had accommodated all the mediocre in the whole bunch in whatever capacity and at least four inexplicable gatherings arranging Biryani. But since he has stopped participating in every little drama, his absence now becomes ''evidence of arrogance''.

This is perhaps one of the established laws of human behaviour among newspaper men: When you stop feeding a particular relationship, the person who was eating and drinking from you will accuse you of starving them. Eventually, the petty manoeuvres become more soap-opera type. For instance, a rumour is carefully planted and then circulated within the office about Mr F’s remaining a bachelor.

A minor editorial error or disagreement is inflated into a question of leadership. Somebody even attempts the conventional office ritual known in South Asia as “Let's see if we can make him look bad without technically saying anything bad.” It is a difficult art. Then again, it requires the delicacy of an astute diplomat coupled with the imagination of a Bengali auntie.
But Mr F had already learnt something by then. He did not need to defeat every accusation. He just needs to keep doing his work. That is his revenge. Not the cinematic kind. No dramatic confrontation. No slammed doors. No speech beginning with “Let me tell you something.”

And here lies the peculiar tragedy of professional mediocrity: People can spend years trying to reduce someone else''s credibility without growing an inch themselves. Mr F hadn't become arrogant because he thinks he is better than everyone.

He now has become selectively unavailable because he finally understands that not everyone deserves equal access to his valuable time, attention, generosity or emotional energy.

And yes, some people will call you arrogant. Let them. If you are polite, they may call you weak. If you are generous, they may call you foolish.
If you are quiet, they may call you a conspirator. If you are successful, they may call you lucky. If you answer them, they may call you reactive. And if you don''t answer them, they may call you arrogant again. At some point, it is important for Mr F to care less about external validation or criticism within the office, since he is mostly surrounded by proven mediocre elements.

The bottom-line however: You do not need to become arrogant. You just need it to become difficult to be misused. Now, there is a difference. You have to be courteous, but don''t need to be permanently available. You have to be generous, but not make your generosity a professional identity.

Respect everyone, but not confuse respect with intimacy. And above all, don't waste your finest emotional energy proving to mediocre people that you are a decent human being. They may already have decided otherwise. So let them.

The British have a wonderfully useful expression for this sort of situation:
“Carry on.” The Bengalis have an equally useful one: “Chhere dao”.
Between the two lies a complete philosophy of survival.

Sometimes you simply smile, straighten your tie, finish the editorial, drink your tea and walk away. Not because I think I am better than everybody else. But because, finally, I have understood that my peace is also a deadline, and some people don't deserve an extension.
